docs.title: ZettelForge documentation
docs.text:
ZettelForge is an open-source, self-hosted memory system for cyber threat intelligence. You store investigation notes, extract CTI entities such as CVEs, actor names, tools, indicators, and ATT&CK techniques, and retrieve the context later by asking a related question.

New here? Install ZettelForge, then follow the Quickstart to store and retrieve your first memory.

docs.title: Two products, one core
docs.text:
There are two products:

  • ZettelForge. You run the MIT-licensed Python package on infrastructure you control. This documentation covers the open-source project.
  • ThreatRecall.ai. You use the managed SaaS instead of operating ZettelForge yourself. Review the current ThreatRecall.ai pricing tiers before you choose a plan.

Choose ZettelForge when you want to operate the memory service and control its local data path. Choose ThreatRecall.ai when you want a hosted service with plan-based limits and features.

docs.title: Get started
docs.text:
ZettelForge 2.8.0 requires Python 3.10 or newer.

python -m pip install zettelforge==2.8.0

The core store-and-recall path runs without a hosted API key. Your first embedding-model use can download model assets. By default, LLM-generated synthesis connects to Ollama at http://localhost:11434 with qwen3.5:9b.

Continue with the Quickstart. If you prefer a browser workflow, follow Use the web interface.

docs.title: Find the right documentation
docs.text:
• Learn the workflow: complete the Quickstart, then ingest your first CTI report.
  • Complete a task: follow a how-to such as Store a threat actor or Set up the MCP server.
  • Look up exact behavior: use the Configuration reference or Memory Manager API.
  • Understand the design: read the Architecture and Two-phase pipeline explanations.

docs.title: ZettelForge — Brand Identity
docs.text:
Canonical reference for agents, designers, and contributors producing any visual artifact for ZettelForge: diagrams, READMEs, slides, social cards, docs, UI.

The brand has one direction: Neural Dark. Light mode exists only as a utility swap for print/GitHub-light-reader parity. Do not invent alternate "themes," "accents," or seasonal variants.

docs.title: 1. The idea in one line
docs.text:
ZettelForge is signal memory — a recall loop, drawn as a nervous system.

Every brand artifact should feel like an instrument panel for a living memory: calm, monospaced, terminal-adjacent, with one channel of neon-green signal punching through. Think threat-intel SOC meets Zettelkasten meets a quiet black-paper notebook. Never corporate SaaS, never playful, never gradient-y.

docs.title: 2. Core visual DNA
docs.text:
Five non-negotiable motifs. If a piece is missing three of them, it is off-brand.

  1. Neuron-chain as metaphor. Pipelines, architectures, and flows are drawn as a vertical chain of circular soma nodes connected by dashed axons. Dendrites (short curves ending in dots) radiate from active nodes. The living stage gets a glow; dormant stages do not.
  2. Single signal color. Exactly one accent — Signal Neon #00FFA3 — used sparingly to mark what is live, current, or you-are-here. Never decorative. If everything glows, nothing does.
  3. Graphite + fog neutrals. Deep near-black backgrounds, graphite card surfaces, cool grey "fog" type. No pure black, no pure white on dark.
  4. Dashed recall trails. Connections between stages are dashed (1.5 7 pattern), never solid. Solid strokes are reserved for node borders and rules. The dash evokes signal pulses traveling an axon.
  5. Monospace is the voice. Code, specs, metrics, chip labels, section eyebrows, and stage indices are monospace. Sans is only used for headlines and body prose.

docs.title: 3. Color system
docs.text: All colors are fixed hex values. Do not introduce additional hues.

docs.title: Neural Dark (canonical)
docs.text: Token Hex Use bg #0A0E17 Page / canvas background card #161B22 Card, panel, stage-description surface node #0D1117 Soma (neuron circle) fill chip #21262D Pill / chip background border #30363D Default 1px borders borderBright #484F58 Node borders, emphasized dividers edgeDim #484F58 Dormant axons + dendrites rule #21262D Section rules fg-1 #C9D1D9 Primary text, headlines, live numerals fg-2 #8B949E Secondary text, eyebrows fg-3 #6B7280 Tertiary / muted metrics, stage subtitles accent #00FFA3 Signal — live stage only pillInk #0A0E17 Text inside a filled accent pill (inverts for legibility)

docs.title: Neural Light (parity only)
docs.text:
Token Hex bg #FFFFFF card #FFFFFF node #F4F6FA chip #F4F6FA border #E5E9F0 borderBright #C9D1D9 edgeDim #C9D1D9 rule #E5E9F0 fg-1 #1F2937 fg-2 #6B7280 fg-3 #9CA3AF accent #5EAE78 (muted sage — neon reads as radioactive on white) pillInk #FFFFFF

Accent rule of thumb: if you are about to use #00FFA3 on more than ~5% of the pixels in a frame, stop and use a neutral instead.

docs.title: 4. Typography
docs.text:
Three families. Two do the daily work; the third is reserved for brand moments.

  • Sans (headlines + prose): Inter, system-ui, -apple-system, "Segoe UI", sans-serif
  • Mono (everything technical): "JetBrains Mono", ui-monospace, Menlo, Consolas, monospace
  • Display (brand only): Neuropol — geometric, wide, slightly sci-fi. Use only for:
  • the ZettelForge / ThreatRecall wordmark and lockups
  • hero display text on marketing surfaces (landing page hero, social card headlines)
  • the single title of a cover slide

Never use Neuropol below ~28px, never for body copy, never for paragraphs, never for UI controls. Its wide forms kill legibility at small sizes. Default tracking 0.01em–0.02em; uppercase for wordmarks.

The web UI bundle ships the font at web/ui/fonts/Neuropol.otf. The token CSS declares it via @font-face in colors_and_type.css as font-family: 'Neuropol' and expects a sibling fonts/Neuropol.otf path. Stack: 'Neuropol', 'Inter', -apple-system, sans-serif (Inter is the fallback so a missing file degrades to the sans headline treatment, not Times).

docs.title: Scale & treatment
docs.text:
Role Font Size Weight Letter-spacing Color Wordmark / hero display Neuropol 44–64 400 0.01em UPPER fg-1 (accent permitted on a single word) Display headline sans 28 700 -0.02em fg-1 Stage title sans 15 600 -0.01em fg-1 Body prose sans 12–14 400 normal fg-2 Eyebrow / section label sans 11 600 0.08em UPPER fg-2 Stage detail / code mono 11.5 500 normal fg-1 Stage subtitle mono 11.5 500 normal fg-3 Stage index (01, 02…) mono 10.5 700 0.12em fg-1 (accent if live) Chip label mono 12 600 normal fg-1 LIVE pill mono 10 700 0.14em UPPER pillInk

Headlines should use text-wrap: pretty where possible. Never use all-caps for prose — only for eyebrows, stage indices, and the LIVE pill.

docs.title: 5. The neural diagram pattern
docs.text:
This is the signature brand shape. Any pipeline, lifecycle, or flow diagram must follow it.

┌───────────────────────────────────────── header ──┐
│ EYEBROW                                            │
│ Display headline                                   │
│ One-line sub                                       │
└───────────────────────── rule ────────────────────┘

         ● ── dendrites (only on active node)
        (●)   soma, r=28, 1.25px border
         │    dashed axon, pattern 1.5 7
        (●)
         │
      ╔══(●)══╗  ← LIVE stage: glow, accent border, LIVE pill
         │
        (●)
         ╲│╱   terminal burst (short lines) on final stage

┌───────────────────────── rule ────────────────────┐
│ STORAGE / EXTENSIONS footer: cards + chip row      │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
• Geometry: soma r=28 (or r=30 for live), soma-center spacing 110px vertical. Description card sits to the right of each soma, left edge at x = soma.cx + 56, height 72px, corner radius 8.
  • Axon: stroke-width 1.5 (or 1.75 entering live), stroke-dasharray "1.5 7", stroke-linecap round, color edgeDim (or accent on the segment entering live).
  • Dendrites: cubic Béziers from soma edge ending in r=2 dots. Only the live node gets colored dendrites. Dormant nodes may get one pair of grey dendrites at the top of the chain (ingestion) to signal "input," and a terminal burst at the bottom (synthesis) to signal "output."
  • Glow: implement with a simple feGaussianBlur stdDeviation=3 + feMerge filter applied to the live soma, its inner dot, and the LIVE pill. Do not apply glow to text.
  • LIVE pill: filled accent, 56×18, radius 9, with a 2.25px inner dot at cx+10 and the word LIVE in mono/700/0.14em tracking, pillInk color.
  • Exactly one stage may be LIVE per diagram. Pick the moment the reader is supposed to feel. If you can't pick one, you're making a reference diagram, not a brand diagram — leave them all dormant.

docs.title: 6. Components beyond the diagram
docs.text:
• Cards: card fill, border stroke, radius 8, no shadow. On dark, shadows disappear — rely on border contrast instead.
  • Chips / pills: chip fill, border stroke, radius 9, mono 12/600 label. Use for taxonomy (extensions, tags, capabilities). Never use them as CTAs.
  • Rules: 1px rule color. Horizontal only. Use to separate header / body / footer zones. No vertical rules.
  • Metrics: right-aligned, mono, fg-3. Example: 66.9% LOCOMO · +33%. Numbers earn their place — cut any that are decorative.
  • Checkered / diagonal backdrops (for showcase pages, not the SVGs themselves): repeating-linear-gradient(45deg, rgba(255,255,255,0.015) 0 2px, transparent 2px 10px) over #05080F. Extremely subtle — should read as "texture," not "pattern."

docs.title: 7. Voice & copy
docs.text:
Short, precise, technical, unshowy. Sentences end early. Verbs do the work.

  • Correct: "Four-stage pipeline; each stage is a node, the axon is the dataflow."
  • Correct: "Validated against LOCOMO. 66.9% recall. +33% over baseline."
  • Incorrect: "Unleash the power of AI-driven memory to supercharge your workflow!"
  • Incorrect: "Discover a revolutionary new way to…"

Eyebrows are UPPER / SLASH / SEPARATED, e.g. ZETTELFORGE / ARCHITECTURE. Stage subtitles name the module, in mono: MemoryManager → FactExtractor. Stage bodies describe the action in present tense, dot-separated: validate → extract entities → resolve aliases.

Never use emoji. Never use exclamation marks. Metrics over adjectives.

docs.title: 8. What to avoid
docs.text:
• Multi-stop gradients, glass-morphism, colored drop shadows.
  • Rounded-corner card with a left-border-accent stripe (the SaaS dashboard cliché).
  • Illustrated mascots, isometric 3D, generic stock photography.
  • Any font that is not Inter or JetBrains Mono in UI surfaces.
  • Any accent color that is not #00FFA3 (dark) or #5EAE78 (light).
  • Solid connector lines, arrowheads, or labeled arrows between stages.
  • "Live" indicators on more than one element per frame.
  • Filler icons next to every heading, stat, or chip.

docs.title: 9. Canonical assets
docs.text:
Paths are relative to the ZettelForge OSS source checkout.

File Purpose docs/assets/zettelforge_architecture.svg Architecture diagram, Neural Dark — canonical docs/assets/zettelforge_architecture-light.svg Same diagram, light parity for print/GitHub light web/ui/colors_and_type.css Token source of truth for HTML surfaces web/ui/fonts/Neuropol.otf Display face — wordmarks and hero moments only docs/brand/brandIdentity.md This document

docs.title: Using the fonts in a codebase
docs.text:
For HTML / web surfaces, import web/ui/colors_and_type.css from the source checkout. It already declares the @font-face for Neuropol and pulls Inter + JetBrains Mono from Google Fonts. Copy both colors_and_type.css and a fonts/ directory containing Neuropol.otf to the target project, preserving the relative path so @font-face resolves correctly.

For anywhere you cannot ship the OTF (third-party slide tools, email, etc.), fall back to the font-display: swap stack — Inter renders in place of Neuropol and the layout stays intact.

When producing a new diagram, copy docs/assets/zettelforge_architecture.svg and mutate it — do not redraw from scratch. Geometry, stroke weights, and font sizes are tuned; drift breaks the family resemblance.

docs.title: 10. Quick agent checklist
docs.text:
Before shipping any ZettelForge visual, confirm:

  • [ ] Background is #0A0E17 (or #FFFFFF for the light parity swap)
  • [ ] Exactly one element uses the signal accent
  • [ ] All technical text is in JetBrains Mono
  • [ ] All connector lines are dashed 1.5 7
  • [ ] At least one soma-node or dendrite motif is present if the piece depicts a flow
  • [ ] No gradients, no emoji, no arrowheads, no third font
  • [ ] Metrics are specific and earn their place

docs.title: Why SQLite + LanceDB (not one or the other)
docs.text:
ZettelForge v2.8.0 uses SQLite as its primary store and LanceDB as its vector index. You get structured notes and relationships from SQLite, plus semantic search from LanceDB, without running a separate database server.

Read this page when you want to understand the trade-off. You do not need it to complete the Quickstart. For exact settings, use the Configuration reference.

docs.title: One note serves two retrieval needs
docs.text:
Threat-intelligence memory combines two kinds of evidence:

  • Structured evidence includes notes, entities, directed relationships, confidence, TLP markings, timestamps, and source-note provenance.
  • Semantic evidence includes passages that mean something similar even when they use different words.

SQLite can store an embedding as data, but ordinary SQL indexes do not provide the vector-nearest-neighbor search that semantic recall needs. LanceDB can attach metadata to vectors, but ZettelForge needs stronger constraints and direct lookups for notes, graph edges, and entity-to-note mappings.

ZettelForge therefore gives each engine one clear role:

Engine Role in ZettelForge Why it fits SQLite Primary record for notes, graph nodes and edges, entity mappings, and enrichment jobs Transactions, uniqueness constraints, indexed lookups, and embedded deployment LanceDB Search index for note vectors, split into one table per domain Vector similarity search and embedded deployment

The split is architectural, not a packaging distinction. ZettelForge remains one self-hosted open-source product.

docs.title: SQLite owns the record
docs.text:
MemoryManager constructs a SQLiteBackend when it starts. The backend creates these core tables:

  • notes stores the full note, its embedding, metadata, links, and provenance.
  • kg_nodes and kg_edges store the directed knowledge graph. Each edge can carry the note_id that supports it.
  • entity_index maps an entity type and value to the notes that mention it.
  • enrichment_jobs records deferred enrichment work.

SQLite enforces uniqueness for entity nodes, graph edges with the same provenance, and entity-to-note mappings. Those constraints prevent common duplicate-write problems without a separate graph service.

The backend enables write-ahead logging (WAL). WAL lets readers continue while a writer commits, which suits a local application that may ingest in the background while you query it. ZettelForge also sets SQLite synchronous=NORMAL: application crashes preserve committed transactions, but an operating-system crash can lose the latest transaction. This is a durability trade-off, not full power-loss protection.

docs.title: LanceDB owns semantic search
docs.text:
ZettelForge creates a LanceDB table for each memory domain and writes a note ID, vector, and bounded search metadata into that table. During recall, LanceDB compares the query vector with stored note vectors. ZettelForge then resolves each matching ID back to the full note in SQLite.

This makes LanceDB an index rather than the authoritative note store. The default fastembed provider generates 768-dimensional nomic-ai/nomic-embed-text-v1.5-Q embeddings in process. The storage design does not depend on the configured LLM provider; language-model extraction and synthesis sit above the persistence layer.

Both engines run in the Python process. By default, SQLite writes zettelforge.db and LanceDB writes vectordb/ under ~/.amem; AMEM_DATA_DIR moves that shared parent directory.

docs.title: A write crosses an intentional consistency boundary
docs.text:
When you call remember(), ZettelForge performs the fast-path writes in sequence:

  1. It constructs the note and embedding.
  2. It commits the note to SQLite.
  3. It indexes the vector in LanceDB.
  4. It writes entity mappings and graph edges to SQLite.
  5. It queues slower enrichment work.

These steps do not share one transaction. Each SQLite storage method commits independently, and LanceDB has its own write path. If LanceDB indexing fails after the first SQLite commit, the note remains in the primary store while semantic recall lacks that index entry. If a later graph write fails, the note can exist without every derived relationship.

That boundary is the main cost of the design. Send writes through MemoryManager.remember() or POST /api/remember so ZettelForge can update both engines. Direct edits to either database bypass the coordination path.

docs.title: Recall blends vector and graph evidence
docs.text:
Recall does more than run a vector query. ZettelForge v2.8.0 follows this read path:

  1. IntentClassifier classifies the query as factual, temporal, relational, causal, or exploratory.
  2. VectorRetriever asks LanceDB for similar notes.
  3. GraphRetriever traverses SQLite graph edges from entities found in the query.
  4. BlendedRetriever min-max normalizes the vector and graph scores, applies the intent's vector and graph weights, and adds the two signals when both find the same note.
  5. Entity augmentation, causal traversal, filtering, and optional cross-encoder reranking refine the result.

The intent policy changes emphasis. For example, a relational query gives graph evidence more weight than vector evidence, while an exploratory query does the reverse. A classification error changes that mix, so it can make an answer incomplete even when every retrieved note is valid.

Retrieval-policy integration is in progress

The v2.8.0 policy map also defines numeric entity_index and temporal weights, but BlendedRetriever currently consumes only the vector and graph weights. Entity and temporal logic runs in separate stages instead of participating in the same weighted fusion. Treat the four-signal policy as an incomplete integration.

docs.title: Why this trade-off is reasonable
docs.text:
The hybrid design gives you three practical advantages:

  • Local operation. SQLite, LanceDB, and the default embedding provider run without database or embedding servers.
  • Traceable retrieval. Vector hits resolve to full SQLite notes, while graph edges retain source-note provenance.
  • Independent repair. The primary record and semantic index have separate responsibilities, so an index problem does not erase the stored note.

You also accept three costs:

  • You must keep two engines consistent.
  • A complete backup must capture both zettelforge.db and vectordb/ from a stable write state.
  • Retrieval quality depends on entity extraction, intent classification, and vector indexing as well as the stored content.

For a self-hosted memory system, this favors simple operation and evidence traceability over a single, more ambitious storage engine.

docs.title: TypeDB product boundary
docs.text:
TypeDB backend selection is in progress

ZettelForge v2.8.0 exposes backend and typedb configuration fields, but MemoryManager uses the storage factory that returns SQLiteBackend. Selecting TypeDB does not replace the primary SQLite path in this release. Do not treat the TypeDB fields as a working ZettelForge backend switch.

ThreatRecall.ai is the separate SaaS product. This page describes ZettelForge's self-hosted storage path and does not imply that both products share the same deployment architecture.

docs.title: Epistemic tiers and confidence
docs.text:
ZettelForge 2.8.0 records two different judgments on every memory note: an editorial tier and a numeric confidence value. The tier can decide whether a note enters synthesis. Confidence records your assessment of the note, but it does not remove the note from synthesis by itself.

Use these fields as policy inputs, not as proof that intelligence is true. The released model stores values that you assign; it does not validate the source or enforce the documented ranges.

Prerequisites: Read the Memory Manager API for note operations and the Configuration reference for the complete synthesis settings.

docs.title: Two judgments answer two questions
docs.text:
Tier and confidence are intentionally separate:

Field Released default Question it answers metadata.tier "B" on a plain Metadata object What editorial role does this source play? metadata.confidence 1.0 How strongly do you assess this note? metadata.stix_confidence -1 What integer confidence did a STIX-oriented integration supply? -1 means unset.

ZettelForge defines three editorial tiers in its default configuration:

Tier Meaning Useful decision rule A Authoritative: high-confidence, verified sources Reserve it for evidence your process has validated. B Operational: working knowledge with moderate confidence Use it for intelligence that supports analysis but still needs corroboration. C Support: low-confidence, inferred, or speculative material Keep it available for investigation without treating it as established fact.

The letter does not calculate the number, and the number does not promote the letter. ZettelForge also does not convert metadata.confidence to metadata.stix_confidence. This separation lets you describe provenance and certainty without collapsing them into one score.

docs.title: Ingestion assigns a starting tier, not trust
docs.text:
The model default and the direct ingestion path use different starting values. A standalone Metadata object starts at tier B. The NoteConstructor used by the ordinary MemoryManager.remember() path creates every note at tier A, regardless of source_type, domain, or text.

That A is an implementation default, not an automatic source assessment. Review the source and rewrite the note metadata when the default does not match your evidence policy. SQLite persists later changes to both tier and stix_confidence.

Tier and confidence validation is in progress

ZettelForge 2.8.0 declares tier as a string, confidence as a float, and stix_confidence as an integer without range constraints. The released model accepts values such as tier D, confidence 1.5, and STIX confidence 101. Validate allowed tiers and numeric bounds in your ingestion layer before you store a note.

docs.title: Evolution applies one confidence cap
docs.text:
Calling increment_evolution() records a revision and sets confidence to the lower of its current value and 0.95. A note at 1.0 therefore moves to 0.95 after its first evolution. A second call increases evolution_count but leaves that confidence at 0.95; the method does not apply repeated decay.

The built-in review predicate returns true when either condition holds:

  • metadata.confidence is below 0.5.
  • metadata.evolution_count is greater than 5.

The boundaries are strict. Confidence 0.5 is not flagged by the confidence rule, and an evolution count of 5 is not flagged by the count rule.

This mechanism is a review signal, not a calibrated probability model. If your workflow needs cumulative decay, corroboration weights, or conflict-aware scoring, calculate that policy outside increment_evolution() and persist the result explicitly.

docs.title: Synthesis filters by tier only
docs.text:
The synthesis generator retrieves notes, removes duplicate IDs, and then keeps notes whose metadata.tier appears in tier_filter. It does not compare metadata.confidence with the generator's confidence_threshold. A tier B note with confidence 0.1 still enters synthesis when B is allowed.

Observed ZettelForge 2.8.0 behavior is:

Call behavior Tiers admitted Omit tier_filter in a direct MemoryManager.synthesize() call A, B, and C Pass tier_filter=["A", "B"] A and B Pass tier_filter=["A"] A Pass an empty list A, B, and C

The last row follows from the generator treating an empty list like a missing value. Pass an explicit non-empty list when you want a restriction.

The configured synthesis default is not wired to direct calls

config.default.yaml and SynthesisConfig default to tiers A and B, but MemoryManager.synthesize() does not load that setting when tier_filter is omitted. The generator uses all three tiers instead. Pass the required filter at each direct call until config-to-runtime wiring is implemented.

docs.title: The operational model
docs.text:
Treat the fields as a small policy vocabulary:

  1. Tier expresses the source's role in your editorial process.
  2. Confidence expresses your current assessment of the note.
  3. Evolution count tells you how often later notes revised it.
  4. Your calling application validates values and decides what requires review.
  5. Synthesis uses only the explicit tier allowlist.

This division keeps ZettelForge flexible, but it leaves enforcement with you. The useful habit is simple: assign deliberately, validate before storage, and pass synthesis policy explicitly.

This page describes the self-hosted ZettelForge model. ThreatRecall.ai is the separate hosted SaaS and is outside this page's scope.

docs.title: LLM budgets, timeouts, and what they cost you
docs.text:
ZettelForge gives five structured-output paths their own configurable LLM budgets: causal triple extraction, synthesis, fact extraction, conversational NER, and neighbor evolution. Each of these paths reads its budget from get_config().llm, and the Ollama provider sends that value as num_predict. The same llm.timeout value flows into ollama.Client(..., timeout=...).

These five paths are not every LLM call site. Intent classification, memory-update decisions, and detection-rule explanations use fixed caps in ZettelForge 2.8.0. Calls that omit a cap use the general llm.max_tokens fallback.

Use this page to understand why the defaults are large, what the reasoning_model flag changes, and how to tune the numbers without editing source code. For the exact config keys, see the llm section of the Configuration Reference.

Before you tune these values, use ZettelForge 2.8.0 and confirm that your configured provider and model already generate responses. The official 2.8.0 configuration defaults to the published Ollama tag qwen3.5:9b, but ZettelForge does not install or start Ollama for you.

docs.title: The token-starvation problem
docs.text:
ZettelForge cannot assume that every generated token becomes useful JSON. Reasoning-style models can spend generated tokens before the final answer, and long prompts can also consume the budget before a valid response is complete.

The observable failure is simple: the provider returns an empty or truncated response. The Ollama provider logs an empty completion as llm_call_empty_response and records the eval_count, done_reason, max_tokens, response_chars, and timing fields. When eval_count reaches max_tokens and done_reason is length, the generation hit the configured cap.

The pre-v2.5.2 defaults were smaller and used a 60 second timeout. The current defaults give generation more room and extend the read deadline so long causal extraction calls can finish instead of timing out.

docs.title: Per-call-site budgets
docs.text:
Each call site reads a different config key, so you can raise the expensive path without increasing every LLM request.

Call site Config key Default Env var Module Causal triple extraction max_tokens_causal 8000 ZETTELFORGE_LLM_MAX_TOKENS_CAUSAL note_constructor.py Synthesis max_tokens_synthesis 2500 ZETTELFORGE_LLM_MAX_TOKENS_SYNTHESIS synthesis_generator.py Fact extraction max_tokens_extraction 2500 ZETTELFORGE_LLM_MAX_TOKENS_EXTRACTION fact_extractor.py Conversational NER max_tokens_ner 2500 ZETTELFORGE_LLM_MAX_TOKENS_NER entity_indexer.py Neighbor evolution max_tokens_evolve 2500 ZETTELFORGE_LLM_MAX_TOKENS_EVOLVE memory_evolver.py General fallback max_tokens 400 ZETTELFORGE_LLM_MAX_TOKENS llm_client.py

docs.title: Why causal extraction gets the largest budget
docs.text: Causal extraction asks the model to return a JSON array of subject, relation, and object triples from up to 2000 characters of note text. It also validates relation names against an allowlist. That is the broadest generation task in the current pipeline, so it gets the 8000 token default.

docs.title: Why synthesis, extraction, NER, and evolution get 2500 tokens
docs.text: These calls produce smaller outputs than causal extraction, but they still need enough budget for structured JSON. Conversational NER and neighbor evolution also retry parsing failures with the same per-call-site budget, so a too-small value can fail both the first attempt and the retry.

docs.title: The shared timeout
docs.text:
llm.timeout defaults to 180.0 seconds. The Ollama provider passes it into ollama.Client(host=..., timeout=...), so it bounds the HTTP read for each Ollama generation call.

Raise token budgets and timeouts together. A larger token budget with a short timeout changes a token cap failure into a read timeout. A longer timeout with the same small token budget still leaves the model capped.

Override the timeout in config.yaml:

llm:
  timeout: 60.0

Or set it with an environment variable:

export ZETTELFORGE_LLM_TIMEOUT=60

docs.title: The reasoning_model flag
docs.text:
When you set llm.reasoning_model: true, ZettelForge runs _apply_reasoning_model_scaling() after it loads config files and environment variables. The scaling step raises these values to minimum floors:

Field Minimum when reasoning_model is true timeout 180.0 max_tokens_causal 8000 max_tokens_synthesis 2500 max_tokens_extraction 2500 max_tokens_ner 2500 max_tokens_evolve 2500

Use it when your configured model needs reasoning headroom and you want to prevent a later config override from dropping the budgets below the verified floors.

llm:
  reasoning_model: true

The flag defaults to false. ZettelForge does not infer it from the model name.

docs.title: Your configured model returns compact answers
docs.text:
If your model does not need reasoning headroom, start with smaller budgets and raise them only when the logs show cap exhaustion.

llm:
  timeout: 60.0
  max_tokens_causal: 2000
  max_tokens_synthesis: 600
  max_tokens_extraction: 600
  max_tokens_ner: 600
  max_tokens_evolve: 600

The matching environment variables let you test a change without editing config.yaml:

export ZETTELFORGE_LLM_TIMEOUT=60
export ZETTELFORGE_LLM_MAX_TOKENS_CAUSAL=2000
export ZETTELFORGE_LLM_MAX_TOKENS_SYNTHESIS=600

docs.title: Your configured model still hits the cap
docs.text:
Raise only the call site that fails. For causal extraction, increase max_tokens_causal and give the request enough time to finish:

llm:
  max_tokens_causal: 12000
  timeout: 300.0

docs.title: Verifying your budgets
docs.text:
The structured JSON log at ~/.amem/logs/zettelforge.log records LLM call outcomes. Set AMEM_DATA_DIR to move the log directory.

At the default INFO log level, inspect empty completions:

grep '"event":"llm_call_empty_response"' ~/.amem/logs/zettelforge.log \
  | jq -r '"\(.model) eval=\(.eval_count) of max=\(.max_tokens) dur_ms=\(.duration_ms)"' \
  | tail -20

At DEBUG level, llm_call_complete records successful calls with the same token and timing fields. If successful calls use far fewer tokens than the configured maximum, you can lower the relevant budget for that call site.

docs.title: How the current behavior evolved
docs.text: Release Change v2.5.2 llm.timeout increased from 60 seconds to 180 seconds. Per-call-site budgets increased to the current defaults. v2.6.0 The five per-call-site budgets moved into LLMConfig, with environment-variable overrides. v2.8.0 The reasoning_model flag added floor values after config load. Structured JSON parsing also began stripping <think> and <thinking> blocks through json_parse.strip_thinking_tags(). Providers still return response text before JSON extraction, so non-JSON callers handle whatever text the provider returns.

docs.text:
• Configuration Reference
  • Troubleshoot ZettelForge

docs.title: STIX alignment in ZettelForge
docs.text:
ZettelForge 2.8.0 is a CTI memory system, not a STIX 2.1 object store. It extracts STIX-adjacent labels from unstructured text and stores them as note metadata and graph entities. ThreatRecall.ai is the separate hosted SaaS and owns native STIX bundle interchange.

This boundary lets you capture intelligence quickly without mistaking a ZettelForge note for a standards-conformant STIX object.

Prerequisites: None. Use the STIX schema reference for exact labels and fields, and the KG edge schema for stored relationship shapes.

docs.title: The mental model
docs.text:
The OASIS STIX 2.1 specification separates threat intelligence into domain objects (SDOs), cyber observable objects (SCOs), and relationship objects (SROs). ZettelForge borrows that vocabulary at three lighter-weight layers:

  1. A memory note keeps the source text and editorial metadata.
  2. The extractor attaches typed strings such as intrusion_set, cve, ipv4, and attack_pattern.
  3. The graph connects those strings with labels such as USES_TOOL, EXPLOITS_CVE, and MENTIONED_IN.

The labels preserve enough structure for CTI retrieval. They do not turn the note, entity, or edge into a STIX object.

docs.title: Where the vocabulary aligns
docs.text:
The released extractor recognizes 19 labels:

Layer ZettelForge labels STIX relationship CTI subjects cve, intrusion_set, actor, tool, campaign, attack_pattern SDO-adjacent subjects Observables ipv4, domain, url, md5, sha1, sha256, email SCO-adjacent values Conversational context person, location, organization, event, activity, temporal ZettelForge context, not STIX objects

The distinction between intrusion_set and actor is operational rather than fully ontological. The deterministic extractor assigns APT, UNC, TA, FIN, and TEMP designations to intrusion_set; it assigns a short built-in list of named groups to actor. recall_actor() searches actor, the compatibility label threat_actor, and intrusion_set so older and newer notes remain findable.

This is alignment, not conformance. A conformant STIX object also carries an object type, a STIX identifier, a specification version, and the common fields required for that object. ZettelForge's extracted strings carry none of that object envelope.

docs.title: Metadata preserves analyst judgments
docs.text:
Each MemoryNote has fields that let an integration retain STIX-adjacent judgments without adopting the STIX data model:

Field Released default Purpose metadata.stix_confidence -1 Holds an integer confidence supplied by your integration; -1 means unset. metadata.tier "B" Records ZettelForge's editorial tier: authoritative, operational, or support. metadata.tlp "" Stores the marking text supplied by a caller. metadata.vuln None Holds optional CVSS, EPSS, and CISA KEV fields for vulnerability notes.

The released Pydantic models store these values but do not enforce their documented numeric ranges. Your importer remains responsible for validating a STIX confidence value before assigning it.

TLP enforcement is in progress

ZettelForge 2.8.0 stores metadata.tlp as an unrestricted string. The released package does not normalize TLP values or apply a TLP ceiling in core recall and snapshot paths. Enforce sharing policy in the calling application. ThreatRecall.ai applies its own tenant-scoped controls in the hosted service.

The separation between stix_confidence and tier is deliberate. A numeric score describes confidence in one assertion. A tier describes the editorial role of the source. Keeping both prevents an authoritative advisory and an unverified report from becoming indistinguishable just because they carry the same number.

docs.title: Relationships stay flexible
docs.text:
ZettelForge writes graph nodes and edges to SQLite and mirrors explicit ingest_relationship() writes to its legacy JSONL graph. The SQLite edge key uses the source node, target node, relationship label, and optional note_id provenance. Repeating the same key updates its properties.

MemoryManager does not validate relationship labels against a STIX schema. That flexibility is useful when raw reports describe organization-specific relationships, but it also means an edge named USES_TOOL is not a STIX Relationship Object. The separate ontology validator exposes a stricter vocabulary, yet the v2.8.0 release does not wire it into MemoryManager writes.

docs.title: Why ZettelForge stops short of native STIX
docs.text:
ZettelForge accepts conversational notes, reports, and observations as raw text. Its deterministic extractor can identify a CVE, ATT&CK technique, threat group, tool, or observable without first constructing a complete bundle. That keeps the ingestion path useful for material that never arrives as STIX JSON.

A native STIX store solves a different problem: preserving object identifiers, required properties, markings, relationship endpoints, and bundle round trips. ZettelForge 2.8.0 does not parse or emit STIX bundles, generate STIX object IDs, or validate SDOs, SCOs, and SROs.

The release also contains legacy hooks that look for an external TypeDB adapter, but the open-source distribution does not ship that adapter or its driver. The default graph path remains SQLite with a JSONL compatibility mirror.

TypeDB integration is in progress

Treat the TypeDB loader hooks as compatibility code, not as a shipped ZettelForge backend. The released adapter tests skip when the absent adapter cannot be imported.

docs.title: The two-product boundary
docs.text:
Use ZettelForge when you want self-hosted memory and retrieval over raw CTI text. Build custom integration code when you need to translate its notes and edges into another platform's STIX model.

Use ThreatRecall.ai when you need hosted STIX interchange. Its current OpenAPI surface exposes authenticated STIX import at /api/ingest/stix and STIX export from recall sessions and threat-agent graph workflows. The service maps those objects to tenant-scoped PostgreSQL kg_nodes and kg_edges records.

That product boundary is the central design choice: ZettelForge optimizes the path from unstructured evidence to recallable memory; ThreatRecall.ai owns the standards-conformant interchange surface.

docs.title: The two-phase extraction pipeline
docs.text:
ZettelForge's two-phase pipeline turns source text into a small set of durable facts, then reconciles each fact with nearby memory. You use it through MemoryManager.remember(evolve=True), remember_with_extraction(), or the OSS zettelforge_remember MCP tool, which enables evolve by default.

The pipeline reduces duplicate, stale, and low-value notes. It does not provide lossless report ingestion in ZettelForge 2.8.0.

Extraction remains in progress

FactExtractor sends only the first 2,000 characters of each input or report chunk to the LLM. An empty or unparseable extraction response produces no facts. remember(evolve=True) then stores the original input through the direct path, but remember_report() stores nothing for the affected chunk. Use a direct, non-evolved write when every source character must be preserved.

Prerequisites: complete the Quickstart and configure a working provider with the LLM settings.

docs.title: Why append-only memory degrades
docs.text:
An append-only memory system stores every report paragraph, repeated claim, and conversational aside. Semantic search still finds related notes, but three problems accumulate:

  • Redundancy: repeated reporting competes for the same result slots.
  • Contradiction: current and superseded assessments appear together.
  • Noise: durable intelligence and temporary conversation receive equal weight.

The two-phase pipeline makes a decision before each extracted fact enters the main store. It keeps provenance through supersession instead of rewriting history in place.

docs.title: Phase 1: extract candidate facts
docs.text:
FactExtractor treats the input as untrusted evidence and rejects recognized prompt-injection patterns before it calls the configured LLM provider. The extraction prompt asks for a JSON array of concise facts with importance values from 1 through 10.

[
  {"fact": "APT28 shifted to edge-device exploitation", "importance": 8},
  {"fact": "APT28 stopped using DROPBEAR", "importance": 7}
]

The parser clamps each importance value to the 1–10 range, sorts the facts from highest to lowest importance, and keeps the first max_facts. remember_with_extraction() then removes facts below min_importance.

Boundary ZettelForge 2.8.0 behavior Input sent to the extraction prompt First 2,000 characters max_facts for remember_with_extraction() 5 min_importance 3 max_facts for remember_report() 10 per chunk Default report chunk target 3,000 characters, split at sentence boundaries llm.max_tokens_extraction 2,500 output tokens

The 3,000-character report chunk target is larger than the 2,000-character extraction-prompt limit. The remaining portion of a chunk does not reach phase 1. This mismatch is the main reason report extraction remains marked in progress.

docs.title: Phase 2: reconcile with memory
docs.text:
For every fact that passes phase 1, MemoryUpdater retrieves the three nearest notes in the same domain. It removes retrieved notes that contain recognized prompt-injection patterns, then asks the LLM to choose one internal operation.

Internal operation Returned status Storage effect ADD added Store a new note with source_type="extraction" UPDATE updated Store the refined fact and supersede the nearest safe note DELETE corrected Store a correction note and supersede the nearest safe note NOOP noop Store nothing

Here, DELETE means that the previous assessment loses authority. ZettelForge does not erase the old note.

If no safe similar note remains, phase 2 chooses ADD without an LLM decision. If the decision response is non-empty but invalid, ZettelForge retries once with an explicit JSON-format instruction. An empty response, a second parse failure, an invalid operation, or an exception defaults to ADD. That failure policy favors retaining a new fact over silently discarding it, but it can create duplicates.

docs.title: How supersession preserves history
docs.text:
The UPDATE and DELETE paths write a new note first. mark_note_superseded() then records the new note in the old note's superseded_by field, adds the old ID to the new note's supersedes list, rewrites both notes, removes the old note from entity-index mappings, and writes a SUPERSEDES temporal edge from the new note to the old note.

Direct MemoryManager.recall() hides superseded notes by default. The OSS MCP recall handler explicitly sets exclude_superseded=False, so MCP recall can return both the current and historical assessments.

This split supports two legitimate views of the same corpus:

  1. Current-only recall gives an operator the active assessment.
  2. Historical recall preserves the chain of evidence and correction for review.

docs.title: What callers receive
docs.text:
remember_with_extraction() returns one (MemoryNote | None, status) tuple for every processed fact. A NOOP result contains None; the other operations contain the new note.

remember(evolve=True) returns only the first tuple even when the pipeline processes several facts. If phase 1 returns no facts, it falls through to the direct write path and returns the directly stored note with status created.

remember_report() returns the combined tuples from all chunks. It returns an empty list when every chunk produces no qualifying facts, and it does not perform the direct-write fallback.

The MCP zettelforge_remember handler returns the first note ID, status, and up to ten extracted entities. When the first operation is NOOP, the note ID is null and the entity list is empty.

docs.title: Failure behavior determines the safe write path
docs.text:
Extraction failures have different consequences:

Failure Observed fallback The extraction LLM call raises an exception Return the first 500 input characters as one importance-5 candidate; the importance filter then determines whether it reaches phase 2 The extraction response is empty or cannot be parsed Return no facts remember(evolve=True) receives no facts Store the original input through the direct path remember_report() receives no facts for a chunk Store nothing for that chunk The phase-2 decision fails Choose ADD

Use evolved writes when deduplication and correction matter and your inputs fit inside the verified extraction boundary. Use remember(evolve=False) or another direct-ingestion path when complete source preservation matters more than LLM reconciliation.

The design deliberately preserves history: new evidence can replace the current assessment without destroying the record that explains how the assessment changed.

docs.title: The Zettelkasten philosophy in ZettelForge
docs.text:
ZettelForge borrows five ideas from Niklas Luhmann's Zettelkasten: small notes, meaningful links, emergent structure, stable addresses, and preservation of old thinking. It translates those ideas into memory notes, a SQLite knowledge graph, and retrieval that combines vector and graph signals.

The analogy is a design lens, not a claim that the software reproduces Luhmann's method. ZettelForge 2.8.0 implements some parts directly and leaves other parts to your ingestion and review policy.

Prerequisites: None. Use the Memory Manager API for exact operations and the knowledge graph edge schema for stored edge shapes.

docs.title: The historical model
docs.text:
Johannes F.K. Schmidt's study, Niklas Luhmann's Card Index: The Fabrication of Serendipity, describes about 90,000 handwritten cards across two collections. Each card received a fixed address. Numbered cross-references connected cards that often sat far apart in the physical collection, while a keyword index supplied entry points.

The important property was not the box. It was the network. A note gained new meaning when a later note linked it into another line of thought.

docs.title: Five ideas in the released system
1. You choose the note boundary
docs.text:
A MemoryNote stores one raw content string with semantic, embedding, link, and lifecycle fields. The direct remember() path keeps the input you give it as one note. remember_chunked() splits longer text on sentence boundaries, while remember_with_extraction() asks an LLM to rank candidate facts and processes each retained fact separately.

This makes atomicity a choice rather than an enforced invariant. A concise fact gives retrieval a precise target. A whole report preserves context but gives each query a larger, less specific unit to rank. Choose the boundary that matches the questions you expect to ask.

docs.title: 2. Links carry direction and provenance
docs.text:
Every recognized entity can become a graph node. A MENTIONED_IN edge connects the entity to the note that contains it. When an actor and another CTI entity occur in the same note, the fast ingestion path can also write relationships such as USES_TOOL, EXPLOITS_CVE, TARGETS_ASSET, and USES_TECHNIQUE.

The relationship label and direction make these edges more useful than a flat tag list. Provenance can connect an edge to its source note, so you can inspect the text behind a graph route.

Relationship inference is in progress

The fast path infers these CTI edges from entity co-occurrence. It does not understand whether the sentence affirms or denies the relationship. In the verified v2.8.0 probe, the text "Sandworm does not use Cobalt Strike" still produced Sandworm --USES_TOOL--> Cobalt Strike. Treat heuristic edges as retrieval leads and validate them against the source note.

docs.title: 3. Structure emerges during retrieval
docs.text:
recall() begins with vector similarity and extracts entities from your query. It follows outgoing graph edges for at most two hops, scores nearer notes more highly, and blends graph and vector scores with weights selected from the query intent. A note found by both signals receives both contributions.

This gives you two paths into the same collection. Similar wording can find a note even when the graph has no route. A named actor, tool, or CVE can open a route to notes that use different wording.

The graph remains directional. A route stored only in the reverse direction is not traversed by this retrieval stage. ZettelForge also drops high-fanout query entities from graph retrieval so a name attached to too many notes does not overwhelm the useful signal.

docs.title: 4. Addresses are stable inside one store
docs.text:
On its first SQLite write, a note receives an ID shaped like note_YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS_xxxx. Rewriting the note preserves that ID.

Graph entities use a different identity. SQLite enforces one node for each exact (entity_type, entity_value) pair and reuses that node across notes in the same store. The node's internal handle is a random node_ ID.

These are local storage identities, not global content identifiers. Capitalization, alias resolution, or a different entity type can produce a different composite key. Deleting and recreating an entity can also produce a new internal handle. Use the typed value as the durable meaning and the internal ID as a store-local address.

docs.title: 5. Supersession preserves explicit history
docs.text:
The verified supersession path keeps both notes. mark_note_superseded() points the old note's superseded_by field to the new note, adds the old ID to the new note's supersedes list, and writes a SUPERSEDES edge from the new note to the old one. recall() excludes the old note by default without deleting it.

The two-phase update path uses this mechanism when an extracted fact updates or corrects an existing note. You keep the prior assertion for audit while current recall favors the replacement.

Automatic evolution is in progress

Direct ingestion can automatically supersede an older note after one shared entity, even when the two notes express different facts. The background neighbor-evolution path also fails to persist on the released SQLite backend because it calls a rewrite method that backend does not expose. Use explicit supersession after review as the reliable v2.8.0 path.

docs.title: Where the analogy stops
docs.text:
Luhmann chose every insertion point and cross-reference. ZettelForge automates candidate extraction, entity recognition, graph construction, and ranking. Automation changes the failure mode: it can scale beyond a handwritten index, but it can also create a confident-looking link from shallow co-occurrence.

Luhmann navigated a fixed-address paper network. ZettelForge adds vector similarity, intent-weighted score fusion, and typed entities. That makes rough language a useful entry point, but the ranking is an information-retrieval result rather than an explanation of why a fact is true.

The practical rule follows from both systems: preserve the source, keep addresses stable, and treat links as routes back to evidence. Structure helps you find a claim; the claim's source determines whether you trust it.

This page describes the self-hosted ZettelForge model. ThreatRecall.ai is the separate hosted SaaS and is outside this explanation's scope.

docs.title: Extend ZettelForge with custom LLM providers
docs.text:
ZettelForge is designed to work without optional packages. The public extension path today is the LLM provider registry. Use this guide to package a provider, register it through Python entry points, and test it without changing ZettelForge's source.

This guide is verified against ZettelForge 2.8.0.

You use this path when you want ZettelForge to call your own local model, OpenAI-compatible gateway, hosted inference service, or lab backend through the same generate() path that built-in providers use.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• ZettelForge 2.8.0 installed; follow the Quickstart
  • Python 3.10+

docs.title: Build a custom LLM provider
docs.text: ZettelForge's LLM layer is pluggable. You can register a third-party provider that the core generate() function delegates to, without modifying ZettelForge's source.

docs.title: How the provider system works
docs.text:
When Python imports zettelforge.llm_providers, the module does two things:

  1. Registers the built-in provider names: local (llama-cpp-python or ONNX Runtime GenAI), ollama, mock, and litellm.
  2. Scans the zettelforge.llm_providers entry-point group and registers any additional providers found there.

The litellm name is registered even when the optional LiteLLM SDK is absent. Calling that provider without the SDK raises an actionable ImportError; install it with pip install "zettelforge[litellm]" before use.

Third-party load failures are logged at DEBUG and do not interrupt the import. Provider names are unique: a third-party entry point cannot replace a registered built-in provider.

docs.title: Step 1: Implement the LLMProvider protocol
docs.text:
Your class must satisfy zettelforge.llm_providers.base.LLMProvider, a typing.Protocol:

from zettelforge.llm_providers.base import LLMProviderConfigurationError


class MyProvider:
    name = "myprovider"

    def generate(
        self,
        prompt: str,
        max_tokens: int = 400,
        temperature: float = 0.1,
        system: str | None = None,
        json_mode: bool = False,
    ) -> str:
        if not prompt.strip():
            return ""
        if max_tokens < 1:
            raise LLMProviderConfigurationError("max_tokens must be positive")
        return "example response"

LLMProvider uses duck typing — no inheritance required. The name attribute is the registry key users reference in config.

For setup failures, raise LLMProviderConfigurationError rather than returning an empty string. The public generate() path propagates this error to the caller instead of hiding the invalid configuration.

docs.title: Step 2: Package and register the entry point
docs.text:
In your package's pyproject.toml:

[project.entry-points."zettelforge.llm_providers"]
myprovider = "myprovider_package:MyProvider"

After you install your package, ZettelForge discovers the entry point when it imports zettelforge.llm_providers. Select the provider in config.yaml:

llm:
  provider: myprovider

docs.title: Step 3: Handle optional SDK dependencies
docs.text:
If your provider depends on an SDK that is not always installed, lazy-import it:

from zettelforge.llm_providers.base import LLMProviderConfigurationError


class MyProvider:
    name = "myprovider"

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._client = None

    def _ensure_client(self) -> None:
        if self._client is not None:
            return
        try:
            import mysdk
            self._client = mysdk.Client()
        except ImportError as exc:
            raise LLMProviderConfigurationError(
                "myprovider requires mysdk. Install with: pip install myprovider-package"
            ) from exc

    def generate(self, prompt: str, **kwargs: object) -> str:
        self._ensure_client()
        return self._client.generate(prompt, **kwargs)

This keeps ZettelForge's core install free of your SDK's dependencies.

docs.title: Step 4: Test your provider
docs.text:
Use reset_registrations() between tests to prevent state leakage:

from zettelforge.llm_providers.registry import (
    available,
    get,
    register,
    reset_registrations,
)


class MyProvider:
    name = "myprovider"

    def generate(self, prompt: str, **kwargs: object) -> str:
        return f"handled: {prompt}"


def test_my_provider_registered():
    reset_registrations()
    register("myprovider", MyProvider)
    assert "myprovider" in available()


def test_my_provider_generate():
    reset_registrations()
    register("myprovider", MyProvider)
    p = get("myprovider")
    result = p.generate("test prompt")
    assert result == "handled: test prompt"

docs.title: What is not a public extension API
docs.text:
ZettelForge contains internal compatibility hooks that let the core vary behavior when SaaS-backed capabilities are present. Treat those hooks as implementation details, not as a plugin system for user packages.

The public boundary is:

  • Use zettelforge.llm_providers entry points for custom LLM backends.
  • Do not create a [project.entry-points."zettelforge.extensions"] group; the source does not scan it.
  • Do not rely on a package-name prefix to trigger discovery. Installing a package whose name starts with zettelforge_ has no effect by itself.
  • If your integration needs a capability that only exists in ThreatRecall.ai, call the ThreatRecall.ai API or design your local code to degrade cleanly.

docs.title: Configure LanceDB vector search
docs.text:
Use LanceDB settings when you need to verify the embedding model, move the local vector index, tune active reranking controls, or plan a safe embedding-model migration.

As verified against the official ZettelForge 2.8.0 wheel and release source on August 22, 2026, the default self-hosted path stores structured data in SQLite and semantic vectors in LanceDB under {data_dir}/vectordb. A clean runtime test stored two CTI notes, created the notes_cti LanceDB table, and recalled both notes.

Retrieval tuning is partially in progress

retrieval.rerank_* and retrieval.entity_max_fanout are active runtime controls. retrieval.default_k, retrieval.similarity_threshold, retrieval.entity_boost, and retrieval.max_graph_depth load into config, but the verified MemoryManager path still uses method or constructor defaults for those values. Pass k directly to recall() today, and treat the other three fields as in progress until the runtime wiring lands.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• ZettelForge installed, or a local ZettelForge source checkout.
  • A local data directory. By default this is ~/.amem; set AMEM_DATA_DIR to use a different directory.
  • Stored notes to test recall against. If you need a minimal note first, see Store a threat actor.

docs.title: 1. Confirm the active embedding defaults
docs.text:
The default embedding provider is fastembed, using the in-process ONNX model nomic-ai/nomic-embed-text-v1.5-Q with 768 dimensions.

embedding:
  provider: fastembed
  model: nomic-ai/nomic-embed-text-v1.5-Q
  dimensions: 768
  threads: 8

Environment variables override the provider, model, URL, and data directory:

export ZETTELFORGE_EMBEDDING_PROVIDER=fastembed
export AMEM_EMBEDDING_MODEL=nomic-ai/nomic-embed-text-v1.5-Q
export AMEM_EMBEDDING_URL=http://127.0.0.1:11434
export AMEM_DATA_DIR=/data/zettelforge

AMEM_EMBEDDING_URL is used when embedding.provider is ollama. The default fastembed provider runs locally and does not call an embedding server.

Verify the embedding output before you rebuild or ingest production notes:

from zettelforge.vector_memory import get_embedding

vector = get_embedding("APT28 uses Cobalt Strike for command and control")
print(f"Embedding dimensions: {len(vector)}")

Verified output:

Embedding dimensions: 768

Before you change embedding.model or embedding.dimensions on an existing store, read Treat SQLite-native vector rebuilds as in progress. Existing vectors are not comparable to vectors from a different model or dimensionality, and ZettelForge 2.8.0 does not ship a working rebuild path for its default SQLite store.

docs.title: 2. Place the vector index with AMEM_DATA_DIR
docs.text:
ZettelForge writes the LanceDB vector index under the active data directory:

{data_dir}/
  zettelforge.db
  vectordb/

The verified default is ~/.amem. This override moves both SQLite and LanceDB data for the current process:

export AMEM_DATA_DIR=/data/zettelforge

In a runtime smoke test with AMEM_DATA_DIR set to a temporary directory, ZettelForge created zettelforge.db, created vectordb/, created a notes_cti LanceDB table after storing a CTI note, and recalled that note through MemoryManager.recall().

docs.title: 3. Tune the active reranking controls
docs.text:
Cross-encoder reranking runs after the initial vector and graph retrieval blend. These fields are read by MemoryManager.recall() at runtime:

retrieval:
  rerank_enabled: true
  rerank_max_candidates: 8
  rerank_doc_chars: 256
  rerank_model: Xenova/ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2
  rerank_threads: 8
  entity_max_fanout: 25

Use these controls when recall returns the right candidate notes but the best note is not ranked first:

Key Default Effect rerank_enabled true Enables the cross-encoder pass. Set false to keep the blended order and avoid reranker inference cost. rerank_max_candidates 8 Limits how many head candidates the reranker scores. rerank_doc_chars 256 Limits how much note text is passed to the reranker. rerank_model Xenova/ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2 Selects the cross-encoder model. rerank_threads 8 Sets ONNX threads for reranking. 0 uses the runtime default. entity_max_fanout 25 Drops query entities that map to too many notes before graph and entity augmentation.

You can disable reranking for a process without editing config.yaml:

export ZETTELFORGE_RERANK_ENABLED=false

docs.title: 4. Treat non-wired retrieval fields as in progress
docs.text:
These fields exist in config.yaml and load into get_config().retrieval, but the verified MemoryManager path does not fully consume customized values yet:

retrieval:
  default_k: 10
  similarity_threshold: 0.25
  entity_boost: 2.5
  max_graph_depth: 2

Current verified behavior:

Field Current runtime behavior default_k MemoryManager.recall() still has a method default of k=10. Pass k directly when you call recall(). similarity_threshold VectorRetriever() still initializes with constructor default 0.15 in the verified path. entity_boost VectorRetriever() still initializes with constructor default 2.5 in the verified path. max_graph_depth MemoryManager still calls graph retrieval with source-level depth 2.

For high precision today, pass a smaller k and ask a narrower query:

from zettelforge.memory_manager import MemoryManager

mm = MemoryManager()
notes = mm.recall("APT28 Cobalt Strike C2", domain="cti", k=5)
print(f"Results: {len(notes)}")

For high recall today, pass a larger k:

from zettelforge.memory_manager import MemoryManager

mm = MemoryManager()
notes = mm.recall("APT28 Cobalt Strike C2", domain="cti", k=25)
print(f"Results: {len(notes)}")

docs.title: 5. Configure LanceDB cleanup
docs.text:
ZettelForge creates a LanceDB version-cleanup helper when MemoryStore initializes and starts it on the first vector write. It reads these fields:

lance:
  cleanup_interval_minutes: 60
  cleanup_older_than_seconds: 3600
Key Default Effect cleanup_interval_minutes 60 Interval between cleanup passes. Set 0 to disable cleanup. cleanup_older_than_seconds 3600 Versions older than this are eligible for cleanup.

For one-shot compaction, inspect first:

DATA_DIR="${AMEM_DATA_DIR:-$HOME/.amem}"
python -m zettelforge.scripts.compact_lance --data-dir "$DATA_DIR" --all --dry-run

Then optimize after you quiesce writers:

DATA_DIR="${AMEM_DATA_DIR:-$HOME/.amem}"
python -m zettelforge.scripts.compact_lance \
  --data-dir "$DATA_DIR" --all --mode optimize --force

The --force flag is required for a mutating run. The script exits with 0 on success, 1 if a table reports an error, and 2 for argument or environment failures.

Default compact mode is in progress

In the standard ZettelForge 2.8.0 wheel, the script's default compact mode exits with code 1 because compact_files() requests the undeclared pylance library. The optimize command above completed against the same standard installation. Use the verified mode until the package declares and tests the missing dependency or changes its default.

docs.title: 6. Treat SQLite-native vector rebuilds as in progress
docs.text:
Do not run scripts/rebuild_index.py against the default SQLite store and assume it rebuilt your vectors. In ZettelForge 2.8.0, that source-checkout helper reads notes.jsonl; it does not read zettelforge.db.

The verification store contained two SQLite notes and a two-row notes_cti table but no notes.jsonl. Both the default helper invocation and its explicit --jsonl form exited with code 0 after reporting Found 0 notes in JSONL. Neither invocation rebuilt the SQLite-backed notes.

An automated SQLite-native rebuild is in progress. Until it ships, keep the existing data directory intact, create a separate AMEM_DATA_DIR for the new embedding model, re-ingest from your original source material, validate recall there, and only then switch your deployment to the new directory. Do not delete the old vector index as a rebuild shortcut.

docs.title: Configure OpenCTI integration
docs.text:
In progress

Native OpenCTI pull, push, and scheduled synchronization are not available in ZettelForge 2.8.0. ThreatRecall.ai supports manual STIX 2.1 exchange and a generic, manually triggered TAXII 2.1 pull. This audit did not connect the TAXII path to a live OpenCTI server, so OpenCTI-specific TAXII compatibility remains in progress.

Use this guide to choose a working handoff path today. You can exchange STIX bundles with ThreatRecall.ai, stage a compatible TAXII collection in ThreatRecall.ai, or write relationships from your own connector into ZettelForge.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• For the ZettelForge path, install ZettelForge 2.8.0 and complete the Quickstart.
  • For the ThreatRecall.ai paths, use a plan with direct ingestion and create an ingest-scoped API key. A read-capable key is sufficient for export.
  • Export a STIX 2.1 bundle from OpenCTI, or obtain a compatible TAXII 2.1 collection objects URL from your OpenCTI operator.
  • Keep OpenCTI and ThreatRecall credentials out of source-controlled files.

docs.title: Choose a path
docs.text: Goal Product and path State Move a bundle from OpenCTI into managed memory ThreatRecall.ai STIX import Verified in the SaaS route tests Move a recall session back to OpenCTI ThreatRecall.ai STIX export Implemented with read, TLP, lifecycle, and redistribution gates Pull a TAXII collection into a review batch ThreatRecall.ai TAXII ingestion Runtime and safety controls verified; live OpenCTI compatibility unverified Feed selected relationships into local memory ZettelForge ingest_relationship() Verified in ZettelForge 2.8.0 Run native or scheduled OpenCTI synchronization Neither product In progress

docs.title: Exchange a STIX bundle through ThreatRecall.ai
docs.text:
1. Export a STIX 2.1 bundle from OpenCTI.
  2. Submit the bundle to POST https://app.threatrecall.ai/api/ingest/stix. Send your ingest-scoped key in X-API-Key and wrap the STIX object in the JSON field bundle. A valid bundle returned HTTP 201 in the route test; a read-scoped key returned HTTP 403 before ingestion.
  3. Run recall in ThreatRecall.ai and retain the returned recall_id.
  4. Request GET https://app.threatrecall.ai/api/recall/sessions/{recall_id}/export.stix with a read-capable key.
  5. Import the returned STIX 2.1 bundle into OpenCTI through the import path your OpenCTI operator supports.

The export route returns application/stix+json;version=2.1 after its policy checks pass. It denies export when source redistribution rules block an object. It also requires an explicit workspace grant when the remaining export contains TLP:RED data. These gates prevent a technically valid STIX handoff from bypassing sharing restrictions.

docs.title: Stage a TAXII collection in ThreatRecall.ai
docs.text:
ThreatRecall.ai contains a generic TAXII 2.1 pull runtime. It does not contain an OpenCTI-specific adapter or a scheduler.

  1. Ask your ThreatRecall operator to allowlist the TAXII host with TAXII_ALLOWED_HOSTS.
  2. Register the feed with POST /api/threat-intel/feeds. Store the collection objects URL in connector_config_ref and set an explicit default TLP and redistribution state.
  3. Trigger POST /api/threat-intel/batches with input_kind set to taxii_2_1_pull and the registered feed_source_id.
  4. Review the staged items, then commit the approved item identifiers through POST /api/threat-intel/batches/{batch_id}/commit.

The pull requires HTTPS outside local development, rejects hosts that are not allowlisted, revalidates redirect destinations, blocks private or reserved addresses, applies an eight-second default timeout, and caps a response at 512 KiB. The service stages returned STIX objects for review; it does not silently commit them.

OpenCTI compatibility boundary

This run verified the TAXII client and staging code with local fixtures. It did not authenticate to a live OpenCTI collection. The current client sends an Accept header but no API token or other authorization credential, so an authenticated OpenCTI TAXII collection is unsupported. Confirm the collection URL and returned STIX objects in your environment before you depend on this path.

docs.title: Write relationships into ZettelForge
docs.text:
Use ingest_relationship() when your connector already reads OpenCTI data and you want to add selected edges to the local ZettelForge knowledge graph.

from zettelforge import MemoryManager

mm = MemoryManager()
mm.ingest_relationship(
    from_type="actor",
    from_value="apt28",
    to_type="tool",
    to_value="mimikatz",
    relationship="USES_TOOL",
    properties={"confidence": 0.85, "source": "opencti-export"},
)

relationships = mm.get_entity_relationships("actor", "apt28")
print(len(relationships))
print(relationships[0]["relationship"])
print(relationships[0]["node"]["entity_value"])

Observed output:

1
USES_TOOL
mimikatz

Use canonical lowercase entity values. The lookup path canonicalizes the query before it reads the graph; the audit found that display-case values such as APT28 did not round-trip through this lookup. Repeating the same source, target, and relationship updates the edge properties and keeps one edge.

This method writes a relationship only. Your connector remains responsible for reading OpenCTI, selecting and normalizing objects, handling checkpoints, and scheduling later runs.

docs.title: Understand the ZettelForge configuration keys
docs.text:
ZettelForge 2.8.0 parses this block from config.yaml:

opencti:
  url: http://localhost:8080
  token: ""
  sync_interval: 0

The matching environment variables are OPENCTI_URL, OPENCTI_TOKEN, and OPENCTI_SYNC_INTERVAL. The defaults are http://localhost:8080, an empty token, and 0 seconds.

These keys do not activate a connector in ZettelForge 2.8.0. Setting a nonzero interval does not start a worker because the release contains no native OpenCTI connector module. Keep the token blank in the YAML file and provide it through the environment if your own connector reads this configuration.
