docs.title: Migrate JSONL data to SQLite
docs.text:
Use this guide when your ZettelForge data directory contains legacy JSONL files and you need to move your notes, knowledge graph, and entity index into the current SQLite store. This path is verified against ZettelForge v2.8.0.

Fresh installations use SQLite and do not need this migration.

Migration tooling is in progress

The v2.8.0 PyPI wheel does not include the migration module named in ZettelForge's startup warning. Run the repository-root scripts/migrate_jsonl_to_sqlite.py file from the v2.8.0 source tree.

Do not use --dry-run as a preview. In v2.8.0, that flag still creates and populates zettelforge.db; it only adds a [DRY RUN] label to the output.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A ZettelForge v2.8.0 source checkout with scripts/migrate_jsonl_to_sqlite.py at its root
  • python3 in an environment that has the ZettelForge dependencies installed
  • Read and write access to the data directory: ~/.amem by default, or the directory selected by AMEM_DATA_DIR or storage.data_dir
  • Enough free space in that directory for both a copy of the JSONL files and the new SQLite database
  • All ZettelForge processes that write to this data directory stopped during the migration

Run every command below from the root of the v2.8.0 source checkout.

docs.title: Run the migration
docs.text:
Set the data directory, then run the repository script:

DATA_DIR="$HOME/.amem"
PYTHONPATH=src python3 scripts/migrate_jsonl_to_sqlite.py --data-dir "$DATA_DIR"

A successful run ends with Migration complete! and reports separate counts for notes, knowledge-graph nodes, knowledge-graph edges, and entity mappings. It writes zettelforge.db with owner-only 0600 permissions and leaves the original JSONL files in place.

The script also copies any files it finds from this list into $DATA_DIR/backup_pre_sqlite/:

  • notes.jsonl
  • kg_nodes.jsonl
  • kg_edges.jsonl
  • entity_index.json

If one of these files is absent, the script warns and continues with the files that exist.

docs.title: Verify the migrated data
docs.text:
First, confirm that ZettelForge can read the SQLite store. Replace actor and apt28 with an entity type and value from your data:

AMEM_DATA_DIR="$DATA_DIR" ZETTELFORGE_BACKEND=sqlite PYTHONPATH=src python3 - <<'PY'
from zettelforge import MemoryManager

mm = MemoryManager()
stats = mm.get_stats()
print(stats["total_notes"])
print([note.id for note in mm.recall_entity("actor", "apt28")])
try:
    mm.store.close()
except Exception:
    pass
PY

Then compare direct database counts with the migration summary:

sqlite3 "$DATA_DIR/zettelforge.db" "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM notes;"
sqlite3 "$DATA_DIR/zettelforge.db" "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM kg_edges;"

docs.title: Roll back and retry
docs.text:
If verification fails, preserve the failed database and rerun the migration from the original JSONL files:

ls "$DATA_DIR/backup_pre_sqlite/"
FAILED_DB="$DATA_DIR/zettelforge.db.failed-$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ)"
mv "$DATA_DIR/zettelforge.db" "$FAILED_DB"
PYTHONPATH=src python3 scripts/migrate_jsonl_to_sqlite.py --data-dir "$DATA_DIR"

The timestamped filename keeps the failed database available for inspection.

docs.title: Move the backup after verification
docs.text:
Keep the backup outside the live data directory after you verify the migrated store:

BACKUP_PARENT="$(dirname "$DATA_DIR")"
BACKUP_DIR="$BACKUP_PARENT/zettelforge-jsonl-backup-$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ)"
mv "$DATA_DIR/backup_pre_sqlite" "$BACKUP_DIR"

Retain both the JSONL source files and this backup until you complete a full release cycle without a migration regression.

docs.title: Why a retry is stable
docs.text: The migration is idempotent for the data shapes it handles. Notes use INSERT OR REPLACE, entity mappings use INSERT OR IGNORE, and knowledge-graph nodes and edges use backend upserts. Re-running the verified fixture kept all four table counts unchanged.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Configuration reference - select storage.data_dir and the SQLite backend
  • Architecture - understand the SQLite and LanceDB storage roles

docs.title: Passive OSINT enrichment
docs.text:
Use ZettelForge's OSINT executor to run registered passive collectors for a single seed entity: a domain, IP address, ASN, or IP block. The executor canonicalizes the seed, invokes matching collectors, validates emitted tuples against the ontology, and writes verified nodes and edges into the knowledge graph when persistence is enabled.

Live collector output is in progress

The executor, registry, canonicalization, validation, dry-run mode, and safety gates are verified in ZettelForge 2.7.0. Live network collectors are best-effort: a collector can return no tuples or record tuple validation errors without aborting the run. Inspect error_count and errors before you rely on a result.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• ZettelForge 2.7.0 installed and initialized.
  • For DNS, WHOIS, and certificate transparency collectors, install the OSINT extra with pip install "zettelforge[osint]". The [osint] extra adds dnspython, python-whois, and ipwhois. The base package already includes httpx, so the BGP collector can run without this extra.
  • Network egress for collectors that contact public services such as DNS resolvers, crt.sh, WHOIS, or BGPView.

docs.title: Supported seed types
docs.text:
The executor accepts five seed types: DomainName, IPv4Address, IPv6Address, ASNumber, and Netblock. Seed type must match exactly — the executor raises ValueError for any other value.

Collectors registered per seed type:

Seed type Registered collectors Current state DomainName cert_collector, dns_collector, whois_collector, builtwith_collector, wappalyzer_collector DNS, WHOIS, and cert collectors run passive lookups. BuiltWith and Wappalyzer are registered stubs and return empty results today. IPv4Address port_scanner, whois_collector WHOIS runs passive lookup. port_scanner is active-gated and returns empty results unless scanning is explicitly enabled. IPv6Address port_scanner, whois_collector Same as IPv4. ASNumber bgp_collector Uses BGPView when reachable; returns empty results on HTTP, DNS, or parse failure. Netblock None Valid seed type, but no collectors are registered today.

You can inspect the registry from Python:

from zettelforge import osint as _osint  # imports collector registrations
from zettelforge.osint import SUPPORTED_SEED_TYPES
from zettelforge.osint.transform_registry import get_transform_registry

registry = get_transform_registry()
for seed_type in SUPPORTED_SEED_TYPES:
    names = [meta.name for meta, _ in registry.find_by_input(seed_type)]
    print(seed_type, names)

docs.title: Run a dry-run smoke test
docs.text:
Run the executor with an empty collector allow-list when you want to verify canonicalization and result handling without network calls or knowledge-graph writes:

from zettelforge.osint import run_osint_collection

result = run_osint_collection(
    "ASNumber",
    "AS15169",
    persist=False,
    collector_names=[],
)

print(result.canonical_input_value)  # 15169
print(result.seed_node_id)           # None
print(result.collectors_run)         # []
print(result.persisted_count)
print(result.error_count)

Input values are canonicalized before any KG writes: "Example.COM." becomes "example.com", "AS15169" becomes "15169". Alternate spellings of the same entity collapse onto the same KG node.

The module also exposes collect_osint(), a compatibility wrapper that delegates to run_osint_collection().

docs.title: Run a live passive collector
docs.text:
Use persist=False first so you can inspect collector output before writing to the knowledge graph:

from zettelforge import osint as _osint  # imports collector registrations
from zettelforge.osint import run_osint_collection

result = run_osint_collection(
    "DomainName",
    "example.com",
    persist=False,
    collector_names=["dns_collector"],
)

print(result.collectors_run)
print(result.tuples_collected)
print(result.error_count)
for error in result.errors:
    print(error.collector_name, error.message)

Collector output depends on the current public records and on network reachability. Treat nonzero error_count as part of the result, not as an exception path; the executor continues with the remaining collectors.

docs.title: Result shape
docs.text:
run_osint_collection returns an OSINTCollectionResult dataclass:

Field Type Notes input_entity_type str Seed type you passed input_value str Seed value you passed canonical_input_value str Canonicalized form seed_node_id str \| None KG node ID for the seed (None when persist=False) collectors_run list[str] Names of collectors that ran tuples_collected int Total tuples emitted across all collectors persisted list[PersistedOSINTTuple] Validated tuples written to the KG persisted_count int Tuples actually written to the KG error_count int Collector or tuple errors (non-fatal) errors list[OSINTExecutionError] Per-collector error detail started_at str ISO-8601 timestamp finished_at str \| None ISO-8601 timestamp

A failing collector does not abort the run. Its error is captured in result.errors and execution continues with the remaining collectors.

docs.title: Dry-run without KG writes
docs.text: Pass persist=False to run collectors and validate output without writing to the knowledge graph. Use this mode for new seeds and for any collector that depends on public network data.

docs.title: Run only specific collectors
docs.text:
Use collector_names to restrict which collectors run for a given seed. The live collector example above runs only dns_collector.

Any name not in the registry is silently skipped — no error is raised for an unknown collector name.

docs.title: Safety controls
docs.text:
Active port scanning is off by default. Without an explicit opt-in, the port scanner collector returns an empty result and sends no packets:

export ZETTELFORGE_OSINT_ACTIVE_SCAN=1

Set this variable only when you own the target network or have written authorization to scan it. Accepted values: 1, true, TRUE, yes. Anything else (including an empty string) keeps scanning off.

Even with the flag set, the port scanner requires python-nmap and the nmap binary. If either is missing, the collector returns an empty result and logs a warning instead of raising.

docs.title: What gets persisted
docs.text:
The executor writes canonical entity values to the knowledge graph. Duplicate spellings collapse onto the same node. For example, AS15169 and 15169 resolve to the same canonical ASN node (15169), and Example.COM. and example.com write to the same domain node.

Each persisted tuple also writes a KG edge with an osint: true property and a source property set to the collector name, so you can later query which collector produced a given edge.

Additional enrichment is in progress

Breach, social, and people enrichment collectors use seed types such as EmailAddress, Alias, and Hashtag that are not in SUPPORTED_SEED_TYPES today. Passing those types raises ValueError. Support for those seed types is in progress.

docs.title: Query what tools an APT group uses
docs.text:
Use the local knowledge graph to list tools linked to a threat actor, then inspect the stored note that supports the result. This workflow uses canonical entity values and does not require a generative LLM or TypeDB.

Current feature state

Canonical APT lookups such as intrusion_set="apt28" are verified. Direct alias shortcuts are in progress: Fancy Bear does not currently find an APT28 entity stored as intrusion_set. Use the normalized value apt28 in this workflow.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Install ZettelForge 2.8.0 and confirm it imports. Start with the Quickstart if you need a working installation.
  • Complete Store threat intelligence about an actor. The output below assumes you stored that page's synthetic APT28 exercise.
  • Run every snippet below in the same Python session.

docs.title: 1. Create a memory manager
docs.text:
Open Python from the same environment and data directory you used to store the note:

from zettelforge.memory_manager import MemoryManager

mm = MemoryManager()

docs.title: 2. List the tools linked to APT28
docs.text:
Query the normalized entity type and value, then keep only USES_TOOL relationships whose neighbor is a tool:

relationships = mm.get_entity_relationships("intrusion_set", "apt28")

tools = sorted(
    {
        rel["node"]["entity_value"]
        for rel in relationships
        if rel["relationship"] == "USES_TOOL"
        and rel["node"]["entity_type"] == "tool"
    }
)

print(f"Tools linked to APT28: {tools}")

if not tools:
    raise RuntimeError(
        "No tool relationships found. Complete the prerequisite exercise, "
        "then query intrusion_set:apt28 from the same data directory."
    )

The synthetic prerequisite produces:

Tools linked to APT28: ['cobalt-strike', 'mimikatz']

The set removes duplicate edges before sorting the values. An empty list means the current store has no matching USES_TOOL neighbor for canonical intrusion_set:apt28; it does not prove the actor uses no tools.

docs.title: 3. Inspect the supporting note
docs.text:
Cross-check the actor and the first returned tool through the entity index. Their shared note is the source context you review before treating the graph edge as attribution:

actor_notes = mm.recall_actor("apt28", k=10)
tool_notes = mm.recall_tool(tools[0], k=10)

matching_ids = {note.id for note in actor_notes} & {note.id for note in tool_notes}
matching_notes = [note for note in actor_notes if note.id in matching_ids]

print(f"Supporting notes: {len(matching_notes)}")
for note in matching_notes:
    print(note.content.raw)

The exercise returns one shared note:

Supporting notes: 1
Synthetic exercise: APT28 deployed Cobalt Strike and Mimikatz. The exercise associates both tools with CVE-2024-3094.

get_entity_relationships() reads direct graph neighbors. recall_actor() and recall_tool() read exact canonical values from the entity index. None of these three calls performs vector retrieval or generates an answer with an LLM.

docs.title: Interpret the result correctly
docs.text:
ZettelForge's fast write path creates these graph edges from entities that occur in the same note. A USES_TOOL edge makes the relationship queryable; it does not independently prove real-world tool use. Review the note's source metadata and underlying report before you treat the result as attribution evidence.

For complete method signatures and return shapes, use the Memory Manager API reference. For multi-hop graph analysis, continue with Run temporal queries.

docs.title: Reproduce benchmarks
docs.text:
Use this page to run the benchmark scripts that ship in the ZettelForge source checkout. Start with CTI retrieval. It is the domain benchmark, uses an embedded CTI corpus, and does not need an external dataset.

The CTI retrieval and CTIBench commands below are verified against ZettelForge 2.8.0. LOCOMO, RAGAS, MemPalace, and MemoryAgentBench are in progress for this how-to. The v2.8.0 prompt-injection guard blocks the three dataset-backed ZettelForge harnesses, and the MemPalace dependency is not installed here.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A ZettelForge 2.8.0 source checkout.
  • Python 3.10 or newer with the ZettelForge runtime dependencies installed.
  • A shell at the repository root.
  • For LOCOMO and RAGAS, locomo10.json at the script default path ~/.openclaw/workspace-nexus/Locomo-Plus/data/locomo10.json, or a path you pass with --data.
  • For CTIBench, the datasets package and network access to Hugging Face. The benchmark directory includes enterprise-attack.json and mobile-attack.json.

Use a disposable checkout when you want a clean working tree. Several scripts write *_results.json files under benchmarks/.

docs.title: Prepare the shell
docs.text:
Run the benchmarks against the checkout source and disable background enrichment so ingestion stays deterministic.

export PYTHONPATH=src
export ZETTELFORGE_ENRICHMENT_ENABLED=false
python3 - <<'PY'
import zettelforge
print(zettelforge.__version__)
PY

The version check prints 2.8.0 for the checkout verified in this run. A configured LLM provider can log provider-specific warnings before the version.

docs.title: Run the CTI retrieval benchmark
docs.text:
python3 benchmarks/cti_retrieval_benchmark.py

This command runs two ingestion strategies over 8 embedded CTI reports and 20 queries. The 2026-08-23 verification run produced these results on this host:

Strategy Notes Accuracy p50 latency full_session 8 75.0% 60 ms chunked_800 8 75.0% 57 ms

Accuracy by category stayed unchanged across both strategies:

Category Accuracy Attribution 100.0% Multi-hop 100.0% CVE linkage 75.0% Temporal 66.7% Tool attribution 40.0%

The script verdict for this run was: same accuracy, chunked mode is faster. Treat that as a local benchmark result, not a release decision by itself.

docs.title: LOCOMO status: in progress
docs.text:
LOCOMO measures conversational memory, not CTI recall. Use the sample command to confirm the harness, dataset path, ingestion path, and keyword judge before you run a larger sample. That quick path does not complete in ZettelForge 2.8.0. The command python3 benchmarks/locomo_benchmark.py --samples 1 --judge keyword loads 10 conversations, 5,882 dialogue turns, and 5 QA pairs, then aborts after 25 sessions. The prompt-injection guard rejects a dataset passage as role_rewrite.

Keep the guard enabled. Do not weaken production ingestion controls to run a third-party benchmark. The benchmark harness needs an upstream, dataset-scoped way to handle this corpus before this path can be documented as working.

docs.title: RAGAS status: in progress
docs.text: RAGAS measures retrieval quality. This sample command uses the same LOCOMO data path and evaluates one QA pair per category. In ZettelForge 2.8.0, python3 benchmarks/ragas_benchmark.py --samples 1 aborts after 25 sessions on the same role_rewrite guard finding as LOCOMO. No v2.8.0 RAGAS score ships from this verification run.

docs.title: Run a CTIBench ATE smoke test
docs.text:
CTIBench ATE tests ATT&CK Technique Extraction. Use a one-sample run first because the adapter loads the Hugging Face dataset and pre-populates ATT&CK technique notes.

python3 benchmarks/ctibench_benchmark.py --task ate --samples 1

The 2026-08-23 smoke test loaded 1 CTI-ATE sample, loaded 293 main ATT&CK techniques from the enterprise and mobile matrices, ingested 292 technique entries, and reported F1: 0.118 with 259 ms p50 latency. Hugging Face logged an unauthenticated-request warning; set HF_TOKEN when you need higher download limits.

docs.title: In-progress benchmark paths
docs.text:
MemPalace comparison is not verified in this run. The local Python environment has chromadb, but it does not have the mempalace package. Treat the MemPalace numbers in benchmarks/BENCHMARK_REPORT.md as historical until you install that dependency and rerun the comparison.

MemoryAgentBench does not complete under the v2.8.0 defaults. A limit-one AR run loads the Hugging Face dataset, then the prompt-injection guard rejects its first context as instruction_override. Treat the MemoryAgentBench numbers in benchmarks/BENCHMARK_REPORT.md as historical until the harness handles the benchmark corpus without weakening production ingestion controls.

docs.title: Historical references
docs.text:
The source checkout also carries benchmarks/BENCHMARK_REPORT.md, which records older April 2026 baselines and a June 2026 performance session. Use those numbers to understand methodology and regression history. Use fresh local runs for current performance claims.

Suite Historical result in source report Current status in this how-to CTI retrieval 75.0% accuracy in earlier snapshots Verified on v2.8.0 at 75.0% LOCOMO Historical full-suite baselines retained In progress: v2.8.0 guard blocks the dataset RAGAS Historical LOCOMO retrieval-quality baselines retained In progress: v2.8.0 guard blocks the dataset CTIBench ATE Historical v2.2.0 F1 baseline retained Smoke-tested only MemPalace Historical comparison retained In progress MemoryAgentBench Historical AR/CR results retained In progress: v2.8.0 guard blocks the dataset

docs.title: What changes your results
docs.text: Factor Effect ZETTELFORGE_ENRICHMENT_ENABLED Set it to false before benchmarking so background LLM enrichment does not change ingest timing. LLM provider availability LOCOMO answer synthesis logs warnings when the configured provider is unavailable. Embedding model This run used fastembed with nomic-ai/nomic-embed-text-v1.5-Q at 768 dimensions. Reranking policy Current source enables cross-encoder reranking with 8 candidates and 256 document characters. Dataset handling LOCOMO, RAGAS, and MemoryAgentBench currently stop on prompt-injection guard findings before scoring. Hardware and thread settings Latency varies by CPU, ONNX thread settings, cache state, and background load.

docs.title: Resolve threat actor aliases
docs.text:
ZettelForge separates entity detection from alias resolution. AliasResolver maps an entity string you already have, such as actor: Fancy Bear, to a canonical value such as apt28. MemoryManager calls the resolver after entity extraction, but the current regex extraction path does not detect every named alias.

For direct lookups, use canonical values. recall_actor() lowercases your input and searches the actor, threat_actor, and intrusion_set index buckets. It does not call AliasResolver at query time. If you have an alias string, resolve it first, then pass the canonical value to recall_actor() or recall_entity().

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• ZettelForge 2.8.0 installed: pip install zettelforge
  • A local data directory. By default this is ~/.amem; set AMEM_DATA_DIR to use a different directory.

docs.title: 1. Understand what the extractor detects before alias resolution
docs.text:
Resolution happens only after extraction returns an entity value:

text -> entity_extractor -> extracted entity values
                         -> AliasResolver.resolve(entity_type, value)
                         -> entity index

The verified v2.8.0 regex path detects canonical APT labels, not every human-readable actor alias:

from zettelforge.entity_indexer import EntityIndexer

extractor = EntityIndexer().extractor

print(extractor.extract_all("Fancy Bear uses Cobalt Strike.", use_llm=False)["actor"])
print(extractor.extract_all("APT28 uses Cobalt Strike.", use_llm=False)["intrusion_set"])

Expected output:

[]
['apt28']

That means a note that only says Fancy Bear does not get an apt28 entity mapping through the regex-only store path. Write source text with the canonical identifier when you need deterministic graph lookup, for example APT28 (Fancy Bear). Use AliasResolver directly when you receive an alias from another tool or user input.

docs.title: 2. Use canonical values with direct lookups
docs.text:
At query time, recall_actor() does a direct index lookup across the actor-related entity buckets:

from zettelforge.memory_manager import MemoryManager

mm = MemoryManager()

# Direct index lookup: use the canonical name.
notes_apt28 = mm.recall_actor("APT28", k=5)

# This searches for "fancy bear" in the entity index.
notes_fancy = mm.recall_actor("Fancy Bear", k=5)

print(f"APT28 (canonical):  {len(notes_apt28)} notes")
print(f"Fancy Bear (alias): {len(notes_fancy)} notes")

recall() performs vector retrieval and graph augmentation. It resolves query entities only when the extractor emits them, so do not rely on it to turn every alias phrase into a graph lookup.

docs.title: 3. Use AliasResolver directly
docs.text:
Use AliasResolver for debugging, pre-processing, or any workflow where you already know the entity type:

from zettelforge.alias_resolver import AliasResolver

resolver = AliasResolver()

# Built-in actor aliases
print(resolver.resolve("actor", "Fancy Bear"))   # apt28
print(resolver.resolve("actor", "fancy-bear"))   # apt28
print(resolver.resolve("actor", "FANCY BEAR"))   # apt28
print(resolver.resolve("actor", "Pawn Storm"))   # apt28
print(resolver.resolve("actor", "Cozy Bear"))    # apt29

# Unknown entity: returns the input lowercased.
print(resolver.resolve("actor", "Volt Typhoon")) # volt typhoon
print(resolver.resolve("actor", "APT28"))        # apt28
print(resolver.resolve("actor", "NewGroup42"))   # newgroup42

Resolve before a direct lookup:

canonical = resolver.resolve("actor", "Fancy Bear")
notes = mm.recall_actor(canonical, k=5)

Built-in aliases are intentionally minimal

ZettelForge ships with six hardcoded actor entries: fancy bear, fancy-bear, pawn storm, and pawn-storm map to apt28; cozy bear and cozy-bear map to apt29. The tool type has no built-in aliases. All other mappings come from your local JSON file or TypeDB.

Input normalization rules:

  • The resolver lowercases lookup input before matching.
  • The resolver replaces hyphens with spaces before the local dictionary lookup.
  • Unknown values return as the original input lowercased.

docs.title: 4. Add custom aliases with entity_aliases.json
docs.text:
AliasResolver loads custom aliases from entity_aliases.json in the default data directory. Use AMEM_DATA_DIR to move this file; otherwise it lives at ~/.amem/entity_aliases.json.

import json
from zettelforge.memory_store import get_default_data_dir

alias_file = get_default_data_dir() / "entity_aliases.json"
alias_file.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

aliases = {}
if alias_file.exists():
    aliases = json.loads(alias_file.read_text())

aliases.setdefault("actor", {})
aliases["actor"]["charming kitten"] = "apt35"
aliases["actor"]["phosphorus"] = "apt35"
aliases["actor"]["bronze silhouette"] = "volt typhoon"

aliases.setdefault("tool", {})
aliases["tool"]["sliver c2"] = "sliver"
aliases["tool"]["cs beacon"] = "cobalt strike"

alias_file.write_text(json.dumps(aliases, indent=2))
print(f"Written to {alias_file}")

Reload and verify:

from zettelforge.alias_resolver import AliasResolver

resolver = AliasResolver()

print(resolver.resolve("actor", "Charming Kitten"))    # apt35
print(resolver.resolve("actor", "Phosphorus"))         # apt35
print(resolver.resolve("actor", "Bronze Silhouette"))  # volt typhoon
print(resolver.resolve("tool", "CS Beacon"))           # cobalt strike
print(resolver.resolve("actor", "Cozy Bear"))          # apt29

Reload after editing

A new AliasResolver instance loads changes from entity_aliases.json. MemoryManager creates its resolver at initialization, so create a new MemoryManager instance after editing aliases.

Use this JSON shape:

{
  "actor": {
    "alias phrase": "canonical name"
  },
  "tool": {
    "alias phrase": "canonical name"
  }
}

Write alias keys in lowercase, space-separated form. The resolver normalizes the lookup input before matching, but it returns canonical values exactly as you store them. Use lowercase canonical values when you want them to match ZettelForge's entity index values. JSON entries extend the hardcoded dictionary. If the same normalized key appears in both, the JSON file wins.

docs.title: 5. Check the TypeDB path
docs.text:
AliasResolver tries TypeDB alias-of relations before it checks the local dictionary for actor, tool, and malware entities. In the default OSS configuration, storage uses SQLite plus LanceDB, so TypeDB is not active and this path returns None.

from zettelforge.alias_resolver import AliasResolver

resolver = AliasResolver()

result = resolver._try_typedb_resolve("actor", "fancy bear")
print(f"TypeDB result: {result}")

print(f"TypeDB available: {resolver._typedb_available}")

canonical = resolver.resolve("actor", "fancy bear")
print(f"Final result: {canonical}")

Expected output when TypeDB is not configured:

TypeDB result: None
TypeDB available: False
Final result: apt28

If TypeDB is unreachable, _typedb_available becomes False for the lifetime of that resolver instance and later lookups go straight to the local dictionary. The resolver returns None instead of raising an exception to the caller.

ThreatRecall.ai keeps its hosted aliases in tenant-scoped knowledge graph records and seed packs. Your local entity_aliases.json configures ZettelForge only; it does not configure ThreatRecall.ai.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
recall_actor() returns empty results for a group I know is in my store.

recall_actor() does not resolve aliases. It looks for the value you pass, lowercased, in the actor, threat_actor, and intrusion_set entity indexes. Use the canonical name:

notes = mm.recall_actor("APT28", k=5)

resolver = AliasResolver()
canonical = resolver.resolve("actor", "Fancy Bear")
notes = mm.recall_actor(canonical, k=5)

If the source text only contained an alias such as Fancy Bear, confirm that the note actually has an entity mapping. For deterministic graph lookup, include the canonical identifier in the stored text, for example APT28 (Fancy Bear).

An alias I added to entity_aliases.json is not resolving.

Confirm the alias key is in the correct entity type bucket, such as "actor" or "tool". Confirm the JSON is valid with python3 -m json.tool "$AMEM_DATA_DIR/entity_aliases.json". Create a new AliasResolver or MemoryManager instance after writing the file.

I need aliases that work for both actor and intrusion_set entity types.

The hardcoded dictionary contains only the "actor" key. If your store uses the STIX-aligned intrusion_set type for APT, UNC, or FIN groups, add the alias under both keys in your JSON file:

{
  "actor": {"fancy bear": "apt28"},
  "intrusion_set": {"fancy bear": "apt28"}
}

docs.title: Run temporal queries
docs.text:
Use temporal queries to see how stored threat intelligence changes over time. ZettelForge 2.8.0 records automatic supersession as a SUPERSEDES edge from the newer note to the older note. You can list those changes, inspect one note's timeline, and choose whether recall returns current or historical notes.

In progress

Automatic supersession creates note-to-note history, but it does not populate actor or other entity timelines. In the verified example below, mm.store.get_entity_timeline("intrusion_set", "apt28") returns []. Native timeline_analysis synthesis is also in progress; ZettelForge 2.8.0 falls back to direct_answer when you request that format.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• You use ZettelForge 2.8.0.
  • You completed the Quickstart.
  • You use the SQLite backend, which is the default backend.
  • You have two related notes in the same domain.

The examples use a fictional APT28 scenario for training. They do not make a current threat-intelligence claim.

Set these variables in the terminal where you run the examples:

export ZETTELFORGE_BACKEND=sqlite
export ZETTELFORGE_ENRICHMENT_ENABLED=false

This keeps the task on the verified SQLite path and skips background LLM enrichment. Recall still uses the configured local embedding model.

docs.title: 1. Store related notes
docs.text:
Store an older report, then store a newer report that shares the same actor and replaces part of the assessment.

from zettelforge.memory_manager import MemoryManager

mm = MemoryManager()

note1, status1 = mm.remember(
    content="APT28 used Cobalt Strike for C2 in January 2026 campaigns targeting EU governments.",
    source_type="report",
    source_ref="vendor-report-jan-2026",
    domain="cti",
)

note2, status2 = mm.remember(
    content="APT28 shifted to Sliver C2 in March 2026, replacing Cobalt Strike in EU operations.",
    source_type="report",
    source_ref="vendor-report-mar-2026",
    domain="cti",
)

print(status1, status2)
print(mm.store.get_note_by_id(note1.id).links.superseded_by == note2.id)

The verified run prints:

created created
True

The second remember() call detects the shared actor, marks the older note as superseded, and creates the graph edge. You do not configure the supersession check per call.

docs.title: 2. List changes after a timestamp
docs.text:
Query the active store that belongs to mm:

changes = mm.store.get_changes_since("2000-01-01T00:00:00")

for change in changes:
    print(
        f"[{change['timestamp']}] "
        f"{change['from']} --{change['relationship']}--> "
        f"{change['to']}"
    )

Each result contains these keys:

Key Type Meaning timestamp str The edge's created_at value. from str The source node as "type:value". relationship str SUPERSEDES or a TEMPORAL_* relationship. to str The target node as "type:value".

The SUPERSEDES result points from note2 to note1: the newer stored assertion replaces the older one. Pass consistently formatted ISO-8601 values because the SQLite query compares the stored timestamp text with your input.

docs.title: 3. Inspect the note timeline
docs.text:
timeline = mm.store.get_entity_timeline("note", note2.id)

for entry in timeline:
    print(f"[{entry['timestamp']}] {entry['edge']['relationship']} -> {entry['to_entity']}")

entity_timeline = mm.store.get_entity_timeline("intrusion_set", "apt28")
print(entity_timeline)

The note timeline contains one SUPERSEDES edge to the older note. The entity timeline prints [] in ZettelForge 2.8.0 because the automatic write path records replacement between stored assertions, not between actor nodes. This note-level model preserves which source assertion changed instead of rewriting the actor as if the earlier evidence never existed.

docs.title: 4. Recall current and historical notes
docs.text:
recall() hides superseded notes by default. Set exclude_superseded=False when you need the historical record.

current_notes = mm.recall(
    query="How has APT28 tooling changed since January 2026?",
    domain="cti",
    k=10,
)

history = mm.recall(
    query="How has APT28 tooling changed since January 2026?",
    domain="cti",
    k=10,
    exclude_superseded=False,
)

print(f"Current notes: {len(current_notes)}")
for note in history:
    status = "SUPERSEDED" if note.links.superseded_by else "CURRENT"
    print(f"[{status}] {note.content.raw[:72]}")

The verified run returns one current note and both notes in history. The phrases changed and since classify this query as temporal. See Retrieval policies for the policy weights and the complete temporal keyword list.

docs.title: 5. Generate an answer from the recalled history
docs.text:
Use the verified direct_answer format:

result = mm.synthesize(
    query="Timeline of APT28 tool changes in 2026",
    format="direct_answer",
    k=10,
)

print(result["format"])
print(result["synthesis"]["answer"])

The first line prints direct_answer. The generated answer depends on your configured LLM provider. Check result["synthesis"]["confidence"] before you use the answer; the controlled run with the mock provider returned a zero-confidence fallback.

Do not request timeline_analysis in ZettelForge 2.8.0. That request returns the direct_answer format instead of a timeline-shaped result.

If you are creating the notes from a report, pass its publication date during ingest. Follow Ingest a news report for the verified remember_report(..., published_date=...) workflow.

docs.title: Working API calls
docs.text: Goal API List store-backed temporal changes mm.store.get_changes_since(iso_timestamp) Inspect note supersession history mm.store.get_entity_timeline("note", note_id) Include superseded notes in recall mm.recall(..., exclude_superseded=False) Check whether a note is superseded note.links.superseded_by Generate an answer mm.synthesize(..., format="direct_answer")

docs.title: Set up the MCP server
docs.text:
ZettelForge ships a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server over stdio. Once wired in, any MCP-compatible AI agent or IDE can call seven tools to read, write, and reason over your local CTI knowledge base without writing a line of integration code.

This guide takes you from a fresh pip install to a working Claude Code or Claude Desktop session with ZettelForge tools available.

Prerequisites:

  • ZettelForge 2.7.0+ installed: pip install zettelforge
  • Python 3.10+
  • An MCP-compatible host (Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor, or any stdio MCP client)

docs.title: Step 1: Verify the server starts
docs.text:
Before touching any config files, confirm the server responds:

echo '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":"2024-11-05","capabilities":{}}}' \
  | python3 -m zettelforge.mcp

The server prints:

{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "result": {"protocolVersion": "2024-11-05", "capabilities": {"tools": {"listChanged": false}}, "serverInfo": {"name": "zettelforge", "version": "2.7.0"}}}

If you get ModuleNotFoundError, check that python3 resolves to the environment where you installed ZettelForge. See Step 3 below.

docs.title: Step 2: Wire in your MCP host
Claude Code
docs.text:
Create or edit .claude.json in your project root (global: ~/.claude/.claude.json):

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "zettelforge": {
      "command": "python3",
      "args": ["-m", "zettelforge.mcp"]
    }
  }
}

docs.title: Claude Desktop
docs.text:
Edit ~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json (macOS) or the equivalent path on your OS:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "zettelforge": {
      "command": "python3",
      "args": ["-m", "zettelforge.mcp"]
    }
  }
}

Restart Claude Desktop after saving.

docs.title: Cursor
docs.text: Open Settings → MCP → Edit config and add the same mcpServers block above.

docs.title: Any stdio MCP client
docs.text:
Point the client at:

command: python3
args: ["-m", "zettelforge.mcp"]

The server reads from stdin and writes to stdout. It prints no startup banner — the first line of output is always a JSON-RPC response.

docs.title: Step 3: Virtualenv paths
docs.text:
If ZettelForge is installed in a virtual environment, the system python3 will not find it. Use the full path to the virtualenv interpreter:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "zettelforge": {
      "command": "/home/user/.venvs/zettelforge/bin/python",
      "args": ["-m", "zettelforge.mcp"]
    }
  }
}

To find the right path:

which python3        # if ZettelForge is in the active venv
# or
source ~/.venvs/zettelforge/bin/activate && which python3

docs.title: Step 4: Verify tools are available
docs.text:
In Claude Code, after reloading:

What tools do you have available from zettelforge?

Claude Code lists seven tools:

Tool Purpose zettelforge_remember Store threat intelligence; extracts entities, evolves memory zettelforge_recall Blended vector + graph retrieval zettelforge_synthesize RAG answer from stored memory zettelforge_entity O(1) lookup by entity type and value zettelforge_graph Traverse the knowledge graph from an entity zettelforge_stats Total notes, entity counts, retrieval count zettelforge_sync Native OpenCTI sync placeholder; in progress

To confirm from the command line:

echo '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":"2024-11-05","capabilities":{}}}
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"method":"tools/list","params":{}}' \
  | python3 -m zettelforge.mcp

The second line of output is the full tools/list response with all seven schemas.

docs.title: Step 5: Test a live tool call
docs.text:
Call zettelforge_stats to confirm the server connects to your knowledge base:

echo '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":"2024-11-05","capabilities":{}}}
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"zettelforge_stats","arguments":{}}}' \
  | python3 -m zettelforge.mcp

A populated store returns something like:

{
  "version": "2.7.0",
  "total_notes": 4594,
  "retrievals": 0,
  "entity_index": {
    "intrusion_set": {"unique_entities": 35, "total_mappings": 2228},
    "cve": {"unique_entities": 16, "total_mappings": 145},
    "tool": {"unique_entities": 6, "total_mappings": 98}
  }
}

total_notes: 0 on a fresh install is correct — you haven't stored anything yet. See the Quickstart for how to populate your store.

docs.title: Configuration options
docs.text:
The server uses AMEM_DATA_DIR for the ZettelForge data directory. It also loads config.yaml or config.yml from the process working directory, then falls back to the packaged default config. No additional environment variables are required to start the MCP server. The server defaults to SQLite backend unless you set ZETTELFORGE_BACKEND first.

To override data directory for a specific host config:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "zettelforge": {
      "command": "python3",
      "args": ["-m", "zettelforge.mcp"],
      "env": {
        "AMEM_DATA_DIR": "/data/cti-memory"
      }
    }
  }
}

docs.title: Backward-compatible entry point
docs.text: Existing .mcp.json configurations that reference web/mcp_server.py continue to work — it is a retained shim that calls the same run_stdio() function. New installations use python -m zettelforge.mcp.

docs.title: TLP and trust boundaries
docs.text:
zettelforge_recall, zettelforge_synthesize, and zettelforge_entity all accept an optional actor field (caller identity string) and tlp_override_reason. Without actor, the server treats the caller as unauthenticated and caps shared content at TLP:GREEN. AMBER and RED content requires both a valid actor and a tlp_override_reason.

All note content in MCP responses is wrapped with content_is_untrusted: true. Your host must treat it as potentially adversarial input.

See the MCP protocol reference for full JSON-RPC request and response schemas and the complete TLP policy.

docs.title: zettelforge_sync and OpenCTI (ThreatRecall.ai SaaS)
docs.text:
zettelforge_sync is listed in the tool schema and appears in tools/list. In the current ZettelForge OSS release it returns a JSON-RPC error response instead of syncing. The tool is present in the schema so MCP host configs do not need to change when native OpenCTI sync ships.

Native OpenCTI pull/push sync is in progress. ThreatRecall.ai currently supports manual STIX 2.1 import and export workflows for OpenCTI, not automatic OpenCTI sync from this MCP tool.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Memory Manager API — call remember(), recall(), and synthesize() directly from Python
  • MCP protocol reference — full JSON-RPC schemas, error codes, and the lazy-singleton lifecycle
  • Integrate with your LLM agent — wire ZettelForge into a custom agent loop

docs.title: Store threat intelligence about an actor
docs.text: Use MemoryManager.remember() to store a CTI note. In this exercise, you store synthetic actor data, confirm the normalized entities, and inspect the one-hop relationships that ZettelForge writes to its local knowledge graph.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Install ZettelForge 2.8.0 and confirm it imports. Start with the Quickstart if you need a working installation.
  • Allow the first run to download the default fastembed model, or warm that model in your local cache before you work offline.
  • Set ZETTELFORGE_ENRICHMENT_ENABLED=false in the Python process environment for this fast-path exercise. This keeps the output deterministic and avoids LLM calls.

The default installation stores notes and graph data in SQLite and vectors in LanceDB. You do not need TypeDB for this task.

docs.title: 1. Create a memory manager
docs.text:
Start Python from a writable directory, then create the default manager:

from zettelforge.memory_manager import MemoryManager

mm = MemoryManager()

docs.title: 2. Store a synthetic CTI note
docs.text:
Keep test data visibly synthetic. This prevents an exercise from looking like a real-world attribution claim.

content = (
    "Synthetic exercise: APT28 deployed Cobalt Strike and Mimikatz. "
    "The exercise associates both tools with CVE-2024-3094."
)

note, status = mm.remember(
    content=content,
    source_type="report",
    source_ref="synthetic-actor-exercise",
    domain="cti",
)

print(f"Status: {status}")
print(f"Note ID starts with note_: {note.id.startswith('note_')}")

The direct write returns:

Status: created
Note ID starts with note_: True

domain="cti" scopes the note to CTI workflows. source_type and source_ref preserve where the note came from; they do not validate the content.

docs.title: 3. Verify the extracted entities
docs.text:
Run the same deterministic regex extractor used by the fast write path:

from zettelforge.entity_indexer import EntityExtractor

extractor = EntityExtractor()
entities = extractor.extract_all(content)

for entity_type in sorted(entities):
    values = sorted(entities[entity_type])
    if values:
        print(f"{entity_type}: {values}")

You get normalized, lowercase entity values:

cve: ['cve-2024-3094']
intrusion_set: ['apt28']
tool: ['cobalt-strike', 'mimikatz']

APT-style designators such as APT28 use the intrusion_set type. Tool names use hyphens, and CVE identifiers use lowercase.

docs.title: 4. Inspect direct relationships
docs.text:
Query with the normalized entity type and value:

relationships = mm.get_entity_relationships("intrusion_set", "apt28")

for rel in sorted(
    relationships,
    key=lambda item: (
        item["relationship"],
        item["node"]["entity_type"],
        item["node"]["entity_value"],
    ),
):
    node = rel["node"]
    value = "<stored-note>" if node["entity_value"] == note.id else node["entity_value"]
    print(f"{rel['relationship']}: {node['entity_type']}:{value}")

The stored note produces these relationships:

EXPLOITS_CVE: cve:cve-2024-3094
MENTIONED_IN: note:<stored-note>
USES_TOOL: tool:cobalt-strike
USES_TOOL: tool:mimikatz

docs.title: 5. Traverse one hop from the actor
docs.text:
Use a one-hop traversal to enumerate the same neighbors as paths:

paths = mm.traverse_graph(
    start_type="intrusion_set",
    start_value="apt28",
    max_depth=1,
)

one_hop_steps = sorted(
    (path[0] for path in paths if len(path) == 1),
    key=lambda step: (step["relationship"], step["to_type"], step["to_value"]),
)

for step in one_hop_steps:
    value = "<stored-note>" if step["to_value"] == note.id else step["to_value"]
    print(
        f"{step['from_type']}:{step['from_value']} "
        f"--[{step['relationship']}]--> "
        f"{step['to_type']}:{value}"
    )

The traversal returns:

intrusion_set:apt28 --[EXPLOITS_CVE]--> cve:cve-2024-3094
intrusion_set:apt28 --[MENTIONED_IN]--> note:<stored-note>
intrusion_set:apt28 --[USES_TOOL]--> tool:cobalt-strike
intrusion_set:apt28 --[USES_TOOL]--> tool:mimikatz

docs.title: Interpret the graph correctly
docs.text:
The fast path infers these edges because the entities occur in the same note. The edges make the note traversable; they do not independently prove that the actor used a tool or exploited a CVE. Preserve trustworthy source metadata and review the underlying note before you treat an edge as attribution evidence.

For complete method signatures and return shapes, use the Memory Manager API reference. To retrieve stored actor knowledge as an analyst, continue with Query APT tool usage.

docs.title: Troubleshoot ZettelForge
docs.text: Use this decision path when ZettelForge fails to start, reads the wrong data, returns no memories, produces a synthesis fallback, or does not connect to an MCP client. Start by capturing the running version and effective configuration; then follow the symptom that matches your failure.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Use ZettelForge 2.8.0. Complete the Quickstart before you diagnose an existing installation.
  • Run every command in the same shell, virtual environment, container, and working directory as the failing process.
  • Keep the Configuration reference and Governance controls reference open. They distinguish parsed settings from settings that the runtime consumes.

docs.title: 1. Capture the version and parsed configuration
docs.text:
Run this snapshot without printing credentials:

python3 -m zettelforge version

python3 - <<'PY'
from zettelforge.config import get_config

cfg = get_config()
for key, value in (
    ("storage.data_dir", cfg.storage.data_dir),
    ("backend", cfg.backend),
    ("embedding.provider", cfg.embedding.provider),
    ("embedding.model", cfg.embedding.model),
    ("llm.provider", cfg.llm.provider),
    ("llm.model", cfg.llm.model),
    ("llm_ner.enabled", cfg.llm_ner.enabled),
    ("retrieval.default_k", cfg.retrieval.default_k),
    ("retrieval.similarity_threshold", cfg.retrieval.similarity_threshold),
    ("logging.level", cfg.logging.level),
):
    print(f"{key}={value}")
PY

The first line must report ZettelForge v2.8.0. Keep warnings from stderr: an env_var_not_found warning identifies an unresolved ${NAME} reference in the loaded configuration.

Treat this output as the parser's view, not proof that every setting is active. In 2.8.0, storage and structured-log paths read AMEM_DATA_DIR directly and fall back to ~/.amem. The base storage factory creates SQLite even when the parsed backend value names another backend. Use the Configuration reference for every other runtime-wiring exception.

docs.title: 2. Confirm the active data and diagnostic files
docs.text:
List the database and logs from the directory the runtime actually reads, then look for LLM and background-enrichment failures:

data_dir="${AMEM_DATA_DIR:-$HOME/.amem}"
printf 'data directory: %s\n' "$data_dir"
find "$data_dir" -maxdepth 2 -type f \( \
  -name 'zettelforge.db' -o \
  -name 'zettelforge.log*' -o \
  -name 'audit.log*' -o \
  -name 'telemetry_*.jsonl' \
\) -print
grep -E '"event": "(all_llm_backends_failed|llm_call_empty_response|enrichment_failed|llm_ner_failed|neighbor_evolution_failed)"' \
  "$data_dir/logs/zettelforge.log" | tail -n 20

No zettelforge.db means the failing process is using another data directory or has not initialized storage. No grep output means the current log contains none of those events; reproduce the failure once and run the command again. Structured events go to logs/zettelforge.log; warning-and-higher events also appear on stderr.

docs.title: Import or version command fails
docs.text: The python3 interpreter in this shell cannot import the same installation as the failing process. Activate that process's environment and repeat step 1. If the version is not 2.8.0, return to the Quickstart and align the installation before changing configuration.

docs.title: remember() raises GovernanceViolationError
docs.text: Use the exception text to identify the control that rejected the write. The 2.8.0 validator checks input type, the maximum-content limit, prompt-injection patterns, and optional PII policy. The parsed governance.enabled and governance.min_content_length fields do not disable or configure those observed checks. Apply the matching control from the Governance controls reference; do not disable governance to work around the error.

docs.title: remember() succeeds but LLM-derived enrichment is absent
docs.text: Compare the effective llm.provider, llm.model, and llm_ner.enabled values from step 1 with the intended configuration. Then use step 2 to find provider, empty-response, or enrichment events. A direct library call defaults to evolve=False and sync=False; set either option only when your workflow requires its additional LLM work.

docs.title: recall() returns no memories
docs.text: Confirm that ingestion and retrieval use the same AMEM_DATA_DIR, and confirm that zettelforge.db exists there. The 2.8.0 base runtime uses SQLite; a parsed backend value does not activate a different store. After ruling out a data-root mismatch, retry the call with exclude_superseded=False. The method defaults to excluding superseded notes. Change retrieval thresholds only after these checks; use the Retrieval policies reference to select a deliberate value.

docs.title: synthesize() returns No specific answer found for: ...
docs.text: Troubleshoot recall() first when the result reports zero sources. When sources exist, search the structured log for all_llm_backends_failed, llm_call_empty_response, and parse_failed with schema set to synthesis. The fallback means the provider returned no usable JSON or raised an exception; it does not prove that retrieval failed.

docs.title: An MCP client cannot find ZettelForge
docs.text:
Test the stdio transport outside the client:

printf '%s\n' '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"tools/list"}' \
  | python3 -m zettelforge.mcp \
  | python3 -c 'import json, sys; response=json.load(sys.stdin); print("jsonrpc={} tools={}".format(response["jsonrpc"], len(response["result"]["tools"])))'

ZettelForge 2.8.0 prints jsonrpc=2.0 tools=7. If this succeeds, set the MCP client command to python3 and its arguments to -m, zettelforge.mcp in the same environment. If it fails, fix the import or version problem first. A successful tools/list response verifies the stdio server and tool registry; it does not initialize storage, embeddings, or an LLM.

docs.title: Upgrade ZettelForge
docs.text: Use this checklist whenever you move between minor releases. For the full list of changes per release see CHANGELOG.md. The current PyPI release verified on 2026-09-09 is ZettelForge 2.8.0.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text: You need Python 3.10 or newer, pip in your active virtual environment, shell access to the ZettelForge host, and enough free space to copy the configured data directory. The examples use the default data directory, ~/.amem. Replace that path if you set storage.data_dir to another location.

docs.title: Upgrade matrix
docs.text: From → To Required action Data migration? 2.7.x → 2.8.0 pip install -U zettelforge (read v2.8.0 notes below) No 2.6.x → 2.7.0 pip install -U zettelforge (read v2.7.0 notes below) No 2.5.x → 2.6.x pip install -U zettelforge (read v2.6.x notes below) No 2.4.x → 2.5.x pip install -U zettelforge (read v2.5.x notes below) No 2.2.x → 2.4.x pip install -U zettelforge No 2.1.x → 2.2.x pip install -U zettelforge + run JSONL → SQLite migration Yes 2.0.x → 2.2.x Upgrade in two hops via 2.1.x is recommended but not required Yes < 2.0 Not supported — export notes manually, fresh-install 2.2.x —

docs.title: 2.7.x → 2.8.0 (passive OSINT + prompt-injection guards)
docs.text: This is a security and enrichment release. No data migration is required.

docs.title: What's new
docs.text:
• Prompt-injection and retrieval-poisoning guardrails (AGE-127). The memory pipeline now treats stored memory, CTI text, query text, and retrieved context as untrusted input at the remember, recall, synthesis, extraction, indexing, note-construction, intent-classification, update, and evolution boundaries.
  • Passive OSINT executor (RFC-016 Phase 1.5). Collector tuples are validated before persistence, OSINT alias caching is scoped to each KnowledgeGraph instance, and organization values are canonicalized to reduce WHOIS/RDAP duplicates.
  • Live OSINT enrichers (AGE-120). WHOIS/DNS, username discovery, breach lookup, and blockchain wallet transaction collectors are available through the optional osint extra. They are opt-in, key-gated where a provider requires credentials, fail closed, and are not triggered automatically by remember().
  • Enrichment job ledger foundation (RFC-018 Phase 0). The release adds durable SQLite job metadata for enrichment queue state and regression tests for the new ledger path.
  • Bulk detection-rule ingest hardening. Bulk Sigma/YARA ingest can defer enrichment and drain once with MemoryManager.flush(). flush() now waits for in-flight enrichment work as well as queued work.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Back up your data directory if you are on a production deployment:

    cp -a ~/.amem ~/.amem.pre-2.8

  2. Upgrade the package:

    pip install -U 'zettelforge>=2.8.0'

  3. If you use passive OSINT collectors, refresh the optional extra:

    pip install -U 'zettelforge[osint]'

  4. Confirm the installed version:

    python -c "from importlib.metadata import version; print(version('zettelforge'))"

docs.title: Operational impact
docs.text:
• No data migration. Existing SQLite, LanceDB, and JSONL-era migrated data stay in place.
  • Passive OSINT remains explicit. Network collectors do not run during ordinary remember() calls. Invoke the OSINT executor from your own workflow and provide provider credentials for key-gated collectors.
  • Stored context is treated as untrusted evidence. Keep the guard wording that ZettelForge adds around retrieved memory when you pass context to an external LLM.

docs.title: 2.6.x → 2.7.0 (memory defense + OSINT + CrewAI)
docs.text: This is a security and OSINT release. No data migration is required.

docs.title: What's new
docs.text:
• Write-time memory anomaly defense (SEC-011 / MemSAD). A new MemoryAnomalyGate scores every incoming note before persistence using embedding similarity and character n-gram divergence. It ships in audit mode — anomalies are logged but writes continue. No operator action is required unless you want block or quarantine mode (see Enable memory defense modes below).

  • OSINT layer — Phase 1 collectors (RFC-016). DNS, WHOIS, BGP, certificates, ports, breach, people, social, and tech collector contracts are now included. Available with pip install zettelforge[osint].

  • CrewAI integration (issue #40). Exposes ZettelForgeRecallTool, ZettelForgeRememberTool, and ZettelForgeSynthesizeTool as CrewAI BaseTool subclasses. Available with pip install zettelforge[crewai].

  • Telemetry attribution. The caller field is now supported in telemetry events. The previous actor field and method arguments remain backward-compatible — existing dashboards and tests are unaffected.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Back up your data directory if you are on a production deployment:

    cp -a ~/.amem ~/.amem.pre-2.7

  2. Upgrade the package:

    pip install -U 'zettelforge>=2.7.0'

  3. (Optional) Install new optional extras:

    pip install 'zettelforge[osint]'    # OSINT Phase 1 collectors
pip install 'zettelforge[crewai]'   # CrewAI integration tools

  4. Start ZettelForge. The memory defense is active in audit mode immediately. Review your log for memory_anomaly_detected events to calibrate before switching to block.

docs.title: Enable memory defense modes
docs.text:
The memory defense requires a calibration corpus before it can reliably gate writes. Until min_calibration_notes domain notes exist (default 50), the gate short-circuits and all writes proceed.

Once your deployment has enough notes, set mode in config.yaml:

governance:
  memory_defense:
    mode: audit       # log anomalies only (default)
    # mode: block     # reject anomalous writes with an error
    # mode: quarantine  # write flagged notes to a separate JSONL file
    quarantine_path: ""   # set a path for quarantine mode

Environment overrides:

Variable Effect ZETTELFORGE_MEMORY_DEFENSE_ENABLED Set to false to disable entirely ZETTELFORGE_MEMORY_DEFENSE_MODE audit, block, or quarantine ZETTELFORGE_MEMORY_DEFENSE_MIN_CALIBRATION_NOTES Minimum calibration corpus size (default 50) ZETTELFORGE_MEMORY_DEFENSE_KAPPA Anomaly threshold multiplier (default 2.0)

See Governance Controls for the full schema and scoring formula.

docs.title: Operational impact
docs.text:
• Audit mode (default): none. Anomalous writes are logged and proceed.
  • Block mode: writes flagged as anomalous return an error to the caller. Turn on only after reviewing audit logs for false positives.
  • Quarantine mode: flagged notes are written to JSONL and hidden from all recall, entity lookup, LanceDB, and graph traversal paths.
  • LLM integration and performance test suites are now explicit opt-in. Set ZETTELFORGE_RUN_LLM_INTEGRATION=1 or ZETTELFORGE_RUN_PERFORMANCE_TESTS=1 to run environment-sensitive tests. The default regression suite (742 passed, 13 skipped) runs without LLM credentials.

docs.title: 2.6.2 (config UI fix — no config changes required)
docs.text:
Released 2026-04-27. Fixes the /config web page.

  • The Save Changes button was silent (called saveConfigForm() and reloadConfig(), neither of which existed). It now submits a real form.
  • Enum-type config fields (backend, llm.provider, logging.level, synthesis.default_format, etc.) render as dropdowns instead of free-text.
  • The YAML editor now accepts both YAML and JSON, and skips redacted *** secrets on submit.

No steps required. Upgrade with pip install -U 'zettelforge>=2.6.2'.

docs.title: 2.6.1 (config API and auth hotfix — no config changes required)
docs.text:
Released 2026-04-25. Fixes three blockers in the RFC-015 web GUI.

  • /config HTML page now renders (was raising NameError on _to_dict and silently delivering a blank YAML body).
  • PUT /api/config now reports nested restart-required fields correctly (was using top-level key comparison instead of dotted-path traversal).
  • /config HTML route is now auth-gated with require_api_guard.

No steps required. Upgrade with pip install -U 'zettelforge>=2.6.1'.

docs.title: What's new
docs.text:
• Configurable content size limits (RFC-014). governance.limits.max_content_length (default 50 MB) prevents oversized content from exhausting memory or blocking the enrichment queue. Set to 0 to disable. Environment override: ZETTELFORGE_LIMITS_MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH.
  • Per-call-site max_tokens budgets moved to config. LLMConfig now exposes max_tokens_causal, max_tokens_synthesis, max_tokens_extraction, max_tokens_ner, and max_tokens_evolve. Defaults match v2.5.2 values.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. pip install -U 'zettelforge>=2.6.0'
  2. Existing config.yaml overrides for llm.timeout continue to work.

  3. (Optional) Override per-call-site budgets:

    llm:
  max_tokens_causal: 12000     # default 8000
  max_tokens_synthesis: 4000   # default 2500
  max_tokens_extraction: 4000  # default 2500

    See LLM Budgets and Timeouts for the full table.

docs.title: Operational impact
docs.text: None if you're on v2.5.2 defaults. Budget values are unchanged; they are now configurable instead of hardcoded. If you were on v2.5.0 or v2.5.1, include the v2.5.2 steps below in the same upgrade.

docs.title: 2.5.x → 2.5.2 (recommended for reasoning-model deployments)
docs.text: Read this first if you run ZettelForge against qwen3 (any variant), nemotron, or any other reasoning model that emits <think>...</think> tokens. Pre-2.5.2 deployments with these models were silently failing every causal-extraction, synthesis, and LLM-NER call — the per-call-site max_tokens budgets were too small for the reasoning phase.

docs.title: What changed
docs.text:
• Per-call-site max_tokens bumped for reasoning-model headroom: causal extraction 300 → 8000, synthesis 800 → 2500, fact extraction 400 → 2500, LLM NER 300 → 2500, memory evolution 1024 → 2500.
  • llm.timeout default bumped from 60 s to 180 s.

docs.title: Operational impact
docs.text:
• Causal extraction now takes 60–140 s per call on a 9B-Q4_K_M reasoning model. remember(sync=True) blocks 1–3 minutes per note. The default async path is unaffected.
  • llm_call_empty_response warnings stop appearing in your OCSF log. See LLM Budgets and Timeouts if they persist.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. pip install -U 'zettelforge>=2.5.2'
  2. If your config.yaml explicitly sets llm.timeout: 60.0, raise it to 180.0 or remove the override.

docs.title: 2.4.x → 2.5.0 (local backend selection + LiteLLM)
docs.text:
No data migration required.

  • Local LLM backend selection (RFC-011). provider: local now supports local_backend: llama-cpp-python (default, no change) or local_backend: onnxruntime-genai for ONNX models. Extra: pip install zettelforge[local-onnx].
  • LiteLLM unified provider (RFC-012). provider: litellm routes to 100+ LLM providers. Extra: pip install zettelforge[litellm].

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. pip install -U 'zettelforge>=2.5.0'
  2. (Optional) Install new extras: 
    pip install 'zettelforge[local-onnx]'   # ONNX local inference
pip install 'zettelforge[litellm]'       # LiteLLM cloud routing
pip install 'zettelforge[local-all]'     # both local backends
  3. Existing config.yaml works unchanged if you are on the default provider: local with llama-cpp-python.

docs.title: 2.1.x → 2.2.x (SQLite migration — data migration required)
docs.text: The default storage backend changed from JSONL files to SQLite. Notes, the knowledge graph, and the entity index now live in <data_dir>/zettelforge.db instead of loose JSONL files.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. pip install -U 'zettelforge>=2.2.0'
  2. Back up your data directory: 
    cp -a ~/.amem ~/.amem.pre-2.2
  3. Run the migration — see Migrate JSONL to SQLite.
  4. Confirm with mm.get_stats() that total_notes matches the migration log.

docs.title: What else changed in v2.2.0
docs.text:
• Causal chain retrieval now works for why did X happen? queries. edge_type="causal" is now filterable if downstream code iterates edges.
  • Memory evolution is on by default once the store has ≥ 3 notes. Pass evolve=False to opt out.
  • STIX alignment. APT/UNC/TA/FIN groups now store as intrusion_set. recall_actor() remains backward-compatible and searches actor, threat_actor, and intrusion_set.

docs.title: Rollback
docs.text:
All of ZettelForge's state lives in the configured data directory plus the installed package. To roll back:

# 1. Pin the previous version
pip install 'zettelforge==2.7.0'

# 2. Preserve the post-upgrade data and restore your backup
mv ~/.amem ~/.amem.failed-2.8
cp -a ~/.amem.pre-2.8 ~/.amem

The package pin does not restore your data. Moving the post-upgrade directory aside keeps it recoverable while the backup restores the matching pre-upgrade state.

docs.title: Use detection rules and the explainer
docs.text:
Use this guide when you have ingested Sigma or YARA rules into ZettelForge and you want an LLM-generated, structured explanation of what each rule detects, how it works, and its false-positive patterns.

This guide covers ZettelForge 2.8.0. The explainer ships in this release. The match-consumer protocol exists, but the built-in consumer registry is empty (see Limitations in 2.8.0).

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• ZettelForge 2.8.0 installed (python -m pip install zettelforge==2.8.0)
  • A configured LLM provider. The explainer calls whatever provider zettelforge.llm_client.get_llm_provider() resolves to. The mock provider returns a deterministic placeholder and makes no network calls, which is useful for testing the wiring.
  • One or more detection rules in Sigma or YARA format

To test the call path without a live model, use the mock provider for the current shell:

export ZETTELFORGE_LLM_PROVIDER=mock

docs.title: How the explainer fits
docs.text:
The explainer is a standalone function. ZettelForge 2.8.0 does not invoke it during ingest: parsing or ingesting a Sigma/YARA rule does not automatically generate an explanation. Call explain() after you have a parsed rule.

The pieces:

  • DetectionRule (zettelforge.detection.base) is the writeable supertype shared by all formats. SigmaRule and YaraRule are subtypes that share its field contract (rule_id, title, source_format, content_sha256, level, status, tags, and others).
  • explain(rule, *, rule_body, provider=None) (zettelforge.detection.explainer) sends the rule to the LLM and returns a RuleExplanation.
  • RuleExplanation is the structured result.

docs.title: Explain a Sigma rule
docs.text:
The end-to-end path is: parse the Sigma YAML, validate it, turn it into a SigmaRule, then explain it.

from zettelforge.sigma import parse_yaml, validate, from_rule_dict
from zettelforge.detection import explain

rule_yaml = """
title: Suspicious PowerShell Download Cradle
id: 11111111-2222-3333-4444-555555555555
status: experimental
description: Detects PowerShell download cradle via Net.WebClient
author: Example
level: high
logsource:
  product: windows
  category: process_creation
detection:
  selection:
    CommandLine|contains: 'Net.WebClient'
  condition: selection
tags:
  - attack.execution
  - attack.t1059.001
"""

rule_dict = parse_yaml(rule_yaml)

result = validate(rule_dict)
if not result.valid:
    raise SystemExit(f"invalid Sigma rule: {result.errors}")

rule, _relations = from_rule_dict(rule_dict)
explanation = explain(rule, rule_body=rule_yaml)

print(explanation.summary)
print("confidence:", explanation.confidence)

validate() returns a ValidationResult with a valid boolean and an errors list. from_rule_dict() returns a (SigmaRule, relations) tuple; the relations describe knowledge-graph edges and are not needed for explanation.

Pass the raw rule text as rule_body. The explainer sends that body, not the parsed object, to the LLM.

docs.title: What you get back
docs.text:
RuleExplanation has these fields:

Field Meaning summary One-line description of what the rule detects mechanism How the rule matches (fields, strings, conditions) threat_model The behavior or threat the rule targets false_positive_patterns List of known benign triggers related_techniques List of related technique identifiers confidence Float clamped to [0.0, 1.0] model Provider name that produced the explanation generated_at ISO 8601 timestamp schema_version RuleExplanation schema version (1.0)

docs.title: Failure handling
docs.text:
The explainer never raises for recoverable conditions. If the LLM is offline, returns invalid JSON, returns an empty response, or rate-limits the call, explain() returns a RuleExplanation with confidence=0.0 and a diagnostic summary (for example explanation unavailable: rate limited or explanation unavailable: llm error (...)). Always check confidence before trusting an explanation:

explanation = explain(rule, rule_body=rule_yaml)
if explanation.confidence == 0.0:
    # degraded result — render the diagnostic summary, do not treat as authoritative
    print("explainer degraded:", explanation.summary)

With the mock provider, explain() returns a canned result: summary="mock provider — no real explanation", confidence=0.0, model="mock:mock". Use it to confirm your call site works without spending tokens.

docs.title: Rate limiting and cost
docs.text:
The explainer enforces an in-process, per-minute cap: 60 calls per minute per process by default. Override it with the ZETTELFORGE_EXPLAIN_RPM environment variable:

export ZETTELFORGE_EXPLAIN_RPM=120

When bulk-explaining many rules, gate enqueue with zettelforge.detection.explainer.rate_limit_ok() before each call; it reports whether the next call fits under the cap without consuming a token. The explainer also re-checks the limit internally, so a caller that bypasses the gate still gets rate-limited rather than overspending.

docs.title: Security model
docs.text:
Rule bodies are untrusted input. The explainer applies several controls before the body reaches the LLM:

  • The explainer wraps the body in a <rule_source untrusted="true"> delimiter, and the system prompt tells the model to treat everything inside as data, not instructions.
  • The explainer neutralizes every </rule_source> sequence so a crafted rule cannot close the delimiter and inject its own instructions.
  • The explainer caps the body at 8192 characters before the call, limiting prompt-injection blast radius and token cost. It marks a longer body with ... [truncated].
  • The explainer discards the verbatim LLM output after coercing its typed fields into RuleExplanation.

docs.title: Limitations in 2.8.0
docs.text:
Match consumers do not ship in 2.8.0

ZettelForge defines a DetectionMatchConsumer protocol and a RuleMatchEvent type for adapting external rule-match events (from a SIEM or detection pipeline) into note writes. ZettelForge 2.8.0 ships the protocol but no concrete consumers — zettelforge.detection.ALL_CONSUMERS is empty. To react to live rule matches, write your own consumer against the protocol.

The explainer is not auto-invoked on ingest

Ingesting Sigma or YARA rules does not enqueue explanation jobs in ZettelForge 2.8.0. Call explain() yourself after ingest completes.

docs.title: Use the web management interface
docs.text:
Use the ZettelForge web management interface when you want a browser view for health checks, search, ingestion, entities, history, logs, and configuration. The interface is part of the self-hosted ZettelForge project. It runs as a single-tenant FastAPI app and serves a JavaScript SPA at /.

The verified startup path is local loopback access. Do not expose the web API on a network interface unless you set an API key and place it behind your normal host controls.

Prerequisites

  • ZettelForge source checkout or installation with web dependencies.
  • A terminal in the ZettelForge project root when you run python web/app.py.
  • Optional stored notes if you want non-empty search, entity, graph, and history views.

docs.title: Step 1: Start the server
docs.text:
Start the web app on an available loopback port:

python web/app.py --port 9000

Expected startup output:

ZettelForge v2.7.0 — http://127.0.0.1:9000

Open http://127.0.0.1:9000 in your browser. If you omit --port, the CLI uses port 8088.

To disable the web interface, set ZETTELFORGE_WEB_ENABLED=false in your environment or set the web.enabled config value to false:

web:
  enabled: false

docs.title: Step 2: Check the Dashboard
docs.text:
The Dashboard is the default route. It shows the left navigation, a header, health tiles, telemetry space, and two action buttons.

The current health API reports:

  • Version and product name.
  • Storage backend.
  • Embedding provider and model.
  • LLM provider, model, and local backend.
  • Enrichment queue depth and queue status.
  • Data directory and knowledge graph node/edge counts.

The Run Compaction and Reload Config buttons are in progress in the current SPA. Reload Config reloads displayed dashboard data. Run Compaction shows a notification only; no compaction API call was observed in the current implementation.

docs.title: Step 3: Use the Search view
docs.text:
Open Search from the sidebar.

The view gives you three actions:

Action What it calls Verified behavior Recall POST /api/recall Returns matching notes for a query. Synthesize POST /api/synthesize direct_answer returns a synthesis object with answer, confidence, and sources. Remember POST /api/remember Stores one note and returns note_id, status, entities, and latency_ms.

Use direct_answer for verified OSS synthesis behavior. The UI also displays synthesized_brief, timeline_analysis, and relationship_map format buttons, but this page does not assert OSS output for those formats.

docs.title: Step 4: Use the operational views
docs.text:
The sidebar exposes these views:

View Current status Knowledge Graph In progress. The API endpoints return nodes and edges, but the browser view showed an empty-graph frontend error in the current runtime probe. Logs & Telemetry Renders log and telemetry controls. Empty environments show zero entries. Ingest Renders single-entry, bulk, and file-ingest controls. The bulk ingest API accepts one or more items. Entities Renders a paginated entity table with type, tier, and text filters. History Renders recent activity with date filters and JSON export. Empty telemetry history shows zero entries. Configuration Renders settings and YAML-editor modes. The server marks restart-required fields through /api/config/meta.

Treat empty tables as normal on a fresh data directory. Store or ingest notes first, then refresh the view.

docs.title: Step 5: Configure API authentication
docs.text:
All API endpoints except GET / use the API guard.

With no API key configured, loopback requests from 127.0.0.1, ::1, localhost, or FastAPI testclient are allowed. Non-loopback requests are rejected until you configure an API key.

Set an API key before you expose the app beyond loopback:

export ZETTELFORGE_WEB_API_KEY=my-secret-key
curl -H "X-API-Key: my-secret-key" http://127.0.0.1:9000/api/health

The same key can be supplied as a Bearer token in the Authorization header. If you bind the CLI to 0.0.0.0 or :: without ZETTELFORGE_WEB_API_KEY, startup fails with a configuration error.

When the browser needs a key, the SPA reads zettelforgeApiKey from localStorage.

  • Configuration Reference — Config keys, including the web: section.
